manader.sub: The darkness, the waiting and the turning of the light
andetag: In almost every tradition that has grown up far from the equator there is a festival of light in December. The Advent candles are lit one at a time, the Hanukkah lights one for each evening, the Lucia flame and the Christmas star, and in China the winter solstice is celebrated with family and warm rice balls. It is as if people everywhere have arrived at the same thing: when the darkness is deepest, no great light is needed. One is enough, and then one more.

At Vreta December is a quiet month. The garden rests, the workshops run slowly and what happens happens mostly indoors and at dusk. The month’s ceremonies are about waiting without hurrying, about keeping vigil on the longest night and about watching the light come back. This year, moreover, the full moon stands high over the snow on the night of Christmas Eve.

intro: The simplest of all winter practices is to light a candle as it grows dark. Not for the atmosphere, but as an act: an acknowledgement that it is dark and that you choose to light. Do it every day in December, ideally in the same place and at the same time.
steg: Choose the place.
A window that faces what is left of the daylight, ideally to the south or west.
Light it at dusk.
In December that is already around three o’clock. Let the candle be the first thing you light, before the lamp.
Breathe three times.
Look at the flame and then out of the window, at the darkness coming.
Say a name.
Someone or something that has given light today. It may be a person, a bird or a line in a book.
Let it burn.
Do not leave it unattended, but let it burn for a while as you do other things in the room.

manader.ingress: December is the deepest breath, the one drawn in before something new can begin. The day shrinks to six hours, and yet it is the month when the most candles are lit.
stat: 6 h 02 min
of daylight at the winter solstice on 21 December. The sun rises at 08.46 and sets at 14.48, and at its highest it stands only seven degrees above the horizon.
dates: The Jewish festival of light begins at sunset on 4 December and lasts for eight evenings. Each evening one more candle is lit in the hanukkiah, in memory of the rededication of the Temple and the oil that lasted eight days.
Two candles in the holder. Advent means arrival, and the fast before Christmas was once as important as Christmas itself.
Buddhist day of remembrance of the Buddha’s awakening under the bodhi tree. Marked with meditation, stillness and sometimes a small tree dressed with lights.
At 01.51. The darkest night of the month and the time for an intention.
St Lucia’s Day (Lucia) and the third Sunday of Advent
St Lucia’s Day falls on a Sunday. The old Lucia night was reckoned the longest of the year, and the candles in her hair are a picture of the promise that the darkness will turn.
The richest meteor shower of the year, with up to 150 shooting stars an hour under a dark sky. The moon is young and sets early, so the night is dark.
Hindu festival for the day when, by tradition, Krishna gave Arjuna the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield. The Gita is read and recited in temples and homes.
The sun turns at 21.49. The day is 6 h 02 min long, the shortest of the year. The same day is World Meditation Day, established by the UN in 2024, and St Thomas’s Day.
The Chinese winter solstice festival, when the family gathers and eats tangyuan, sweet rice balls in warm soup, as a picture of togetherness.
Christmas Eve and the Winter Moon
Full moon at 02.28, the night before Christmas Eve. The moon stands high over the snow all Christmas night, as it did for those going to the early Christmas service in the old days.
The birth of Christ. Julotta, the early Christmas morning service that once went in darkness with torches and lanterns, is held in many churches early in the morning.
A public holiday. A day for rest and visits, once the first great day of Christmas has settled.
An African-American festival of seven days, with a candle for each of seven principles, such as unity, creativity and faith.
The old year is left behind. In many homes New Year’s tin is cast, in others what is to be let go is written down and burned.
events: From the first evening and on all eight evenings, anyone who celebrates Hanukkah is welcome to light their candles in the orangery, and we offer doughnuts from the wood oven. Whoever carries the tradition leads it.
An hour in the still room on the second Sunday of Advent: a candle, a song and silence. Then glögg and gingersnaps in the café.
An evening of sitting meditation in the spirit hall, in short sessions of twenty minutes, with slow walking in between. No experience needed.
An evening with a candle and a notebook. Each person writes down a direction for the winter and lays it under a stone on the altar.
A Lucia procession with candles walks from the cottage down to the pond in the blue hour. Coffee, saffron buns (lussekatter) and silence by the ice.
The Geminids from the meadow. Reindeer skins, blankets, hot chocolate and a short tour of the winter sky.
An evening with the frame drum in the spirit hall. The drum beats a steady rhythm, and each person lies or sits with a question about the passing year.
From sunset at 14.48 to sunrise at 08.47. The fire in the meadow is kept alive all night, and we take turns to keep watch, tell stories and rest.
A short while by the pond early on the morning of Christmas Eve, when the full moon stands in the west over the snow. Then each person goes home to their own Christmas.
New Year’s Eve by the fire
What is to be let go is written on paper and laid in the fire. What is to be carried on is said aloud or carried in silence.
fraga: What do I need to rest from before the light comes back?
The question is not about what you should start, but about what you can let be.
ord: The word means both the medicine and the healing. In the Andes a healer is a hampiq, the one who heals. Healing is not that something disappears, but that it finds its rightful place.
manader.hand: One candle is enough. Then one more.

manader.sub: Silence, ice and the slow return of the light
andetag: After December, January is a relief. The festivities are over, the tree is carried out and nothing needs preparing. It is the quietest month of the year, and it is a gift to whoever accepts it. Many traditions have their fasts and cleansings at the start of the year, and that is no accident: when there is nothing to harvest and nothing to sow, it is time to look inward.

At Vreta, January begins with a walk in silence. Then come the shooting stars, the new moon’s intention and the Ice Moon sauna, when the full moon stands over the pond and the ice hole has been cut. Otherwise it is a month for sitting still, reading, planning and watching the light come back.

intro: January is the best month to begin sitting still, since there is not much else to do. Ten minutes is enough. It is not about emptying the mind, but about noticing what is there.
steg: Sit comfortably.
On a chair with your feet on the floor, or on a cushion. Back straight but not stiff.
Set a timer.
Ten minutes. Then you need not look.
Follow the breath.
Notice the air going in and out through your nose. Count to ten if you like, and begin again.
Let the thoughts come.
They come, like snowflakes. Watch them land and melt, and return to the breath.
Finish slowly.
Open your eyes, look around and quietly name what you see.

manader.ingress: January is a breath held. The ice settles, sound grows softer and the light grows by a few minutes a day. Whoever is still can hear it.
stat: 8 h 01 min
of daylight on 31 January in Uppsala, against 6 h 11 min on 1 January. In a month the day grows by 1 h 49 min.
dates: The first day of the year and a public holiday. At Vreta it begins with a walk in silence along the shore of Ekoln and breakfast at the long table in the orangery.
The first meteor shower of the year, with up to a hundred or so shooting stars an hour in good conditions. The moon is almost new, so the night is dark. Best after midnight and towards morning.
Venus stands furthest from the sun, at greatest western elongation, on 3–4 January. It shines brighter than anything else in the sky except the sun and the moon.
A public holiday and the day of the three wise men. The Christmas tree may stay up another week, but the star is taken down and the candlesticks packed away.
The Orthodox Church celebrates Christmas by the Julian calendar. The same evening the moon is new – a good night to put an intention for the year into words.
"On St Knut’s Day Christmas is danced out." The tree is carried out, and the needles go to the compost. Uppsala’s schools begin the spring term the same day.
A Punjabi winter fire on the evening before Makar Sankranti. People gather round a bonfire, throw sesame, peanuts and popcorn into the fire and dance bhangra.

Hindu harvest festival when the sun enters Capricorn and the days grow longer. In the north kites are flown and sesame sweets shared; in Tamil Nadu the rice dish pongal is boiled until it boils over – a sign of abundance.
Full moon at 13.17, and the closest of the year. It rises over the birches in the north-east in the afternoon and shines over the snow all night.
Tamil Hindu festival for the god Murugan at the full moon in the month of Thai. Pilgrims carry kavadi, often heavy burdens, in thanks and penance.
International day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust, on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1945. A candle is lit in many schools and churches.
The moon wanes. The nights grow dark again before February, and the starry sky is at its clearest.
events: A walk along the shore of Ekoln and through the broadleaf woods to the old oak, without words. We finish with a simple breakfast at the long table in the orangery. Open to all.
The Quadrantids from the meadow. Reindeer skins, blankets, hot chocolate and a short tour of the winter sky before the lanterns are put out.
An evening in the spirit hall with a candle and a notebook. Each person writes down a direction for the year – not a goal – and lays it under a stone on the altar.
St Knut’s Day and the Christmas-tree fire
The trees from the place and the neighbours’ homes are gathered. The branches become mulch and chippings, the trunks become bean poles – and a small bonfire at the fire place as darkness falls.
A whole day in silence, from 9 to 4. Sitting and walking meditation, a simple wordless lunch and a walk to the old oak. Booking in advance.
Full moon, a fired sauna and a winter dip in the ice hole. With the same simple rules as always: never alone, never after alcohol, always someone on land.
A light for those who remember
On Holocaust Memorial Day a candle is lit in the window of the cottage. Anyone who wishes may come by and light one of their own.
fraga: What do I hear when it falls silent?
Not only the sounds around me, but also what they usually drown out.
ord: In the Andean tradition sami is the light, refined energy, like nectar, and hucha the heavy. Hucha is not evil, only energy that has not been allowed to move. The earth, Pachamama, is said to eat hucha gladly.

andetag: February is the month of waiting. The day grows by more than two hours, but the cold holds on. In the Celtic tradition 1 February is Imbolc, the first festival of spring, when the ewes lambed and candles were lit for Brigid. In the Christian church it is Candlemas (kyndelsmäss), the mass of light, when the year’s candles were blessed. In the same month come the Sámi National Day, the Chinese lunar new year and the start of Ramadan.

At Vreta new beeswax candles are dipped for Candlemas, and the first seeds are sown in the cottage window. They are small acts, but they point forward. The Light Moon on 20–21 February is faintly eclipsed in the penumbra just after midnight.

intro: An intention is easier to hold on to if it has a body. In February, when the first seeds are sown indoors, the intention and the seed can become the same thing.
steg: Choose a seed.
Something that can be sown now: chilli, leek, a flower. Hold it in your palm.
Put a direction into words.
Not a goal, but something you want to grow – more patience, more time outdoors, a conversation you want to have.
Say it quietly to the seed.
It sounds strange, but it helps to say it somewhere.
Sow it.
In a pot of soil, in a window where you see it every day.
Watch it sprout.
When the first leaf comes, ask yourself whether your intention has also begun to move.

manader.ingress: In February the light comes back long before the warmth. It glitters on the snow crust and shines in the windows, and whoever has waited all winter begins to wait for something else.
stat: 10 h 27 min
of daylight on 28 February in Uppsala, against 8 h 06 min on 1 February. In a month the day grows by 2 h 21 min.
dates: The Celtic spring festival, midway between the winter solstice and the spring equinox. Candles are lit for Brigid, saint of fire, poetry and wells.

The winter market in Jokkmokk has been held since 1605 and gathers trade, handicraft and reindeer caravans in the cold. A reminder that winter in the north is a season of its own and not only a wait for spring.
The day commemorates the first Sámi national assembly in Trondheim in 1917, this year 110 years ago. The Sámi flag is raised in many places across the country, Vreta included.
New moon and lunar new year
The moon is new at 16.56. The same day the lunar new year begins in China and much of East Asia – the Year of the Sheep, also called the Year of the Goat.
The Feast of the Purification of the Virgin Mary and the old mass of light, when the church’s candles were blessed for the year. "At Candlemas the farmer should have half his fodder left."
The Islamic month of fasting begins around these days, once the new crescent moon has been sighted. The sun sets just before half past four, and then the fast is broken with iftar.
Tibetan New Year, a Buddhist new year with cleansing of the house, prayers, offerings at the altar and festivities for fifteen days.
The last day before Lent and the day of semlor, the cream-filled cardamom buns. At Vreta they are baked in the wood-fired oven.
The Christian fast before Easter begins – forty days until Easter Saturday, Sundays not counted.
Jupiter stands opposite the sun and shines all night in Leo, brighter than any star.
Hindu spring festival for Saraswati, goddess of knowledge, music and the arts. People dress in yellow, and children often write their first letters on this day.
The day of friendship and love. As it grows dark the half moon stands close to the Pleiades high in the south.
The Mahayana Buddhists’ day of remembrance for the Buddha’s passing and final liberation. A day for stillness and for remembering that all things pass. Some mark it on 8 February.
Full moon at 00.23 and a penumbral eclipse, greatest at 00.13. At most the moon gains a faint grey veil over one edge.

The Theravada Buddhists’ Sangha Day at the full moon, in memory of when 1,250 monks gathered with the Buddha without having been summoned. People walk three times round the temple with candles, flowers and incense.
"Matthias breaks the ice; if there is no ice, he makes ice." Folk belief expected a change in the weather around this day.
events: A short ceremony in the cottage at Imbolc: a cross is plaited from straw, and a plate of bread and milk is set in the window for whoever passes by.
The new moon’s intention and lunar new year
New moon at 16.56 and Chinese New Year the same day. We write an intention for the spring and eat dumplings in the café.
We dip candles from the wax of the place’s own beehives in the workshop during the afternoon. At dusk they are carried to the spirit hall and lit together. For all ages.
Anyone fasting during Ramadan is welcome to break the fast at the long table in the orangery. The sun sets at 16.37. Whoever carries the tradition leads the evening.

Full moon and eclipse, and Mars close to the earth the same weekend. We gather at the fire place just before midnight with binoculars and blankets, and the sauna is fired for anyone who wants to end the night in the warmth.
A walk in silence along the shore of Ekoln to the old oak, with a question to carry. We meet at the birch arch at 10.
fraga: What am I waiting for – and what can I already begin?
The light does not wait for the warmth. It comes first.
ord: Yanantin is the idea that opposites do not fight but complete one another: light and dark, man and woman, sun and moon, right and left. Harmony is not that one wins, but that both have room.
manader.hand: The light first – the warmth will come.

manader.sub: Equinox, sap and an early Easter
andetag: The spring equinox on 20 March is one of the year’s two points of balance: twelve hours of light, twelve hours of dark. The same day Nowruz, the Persian New Year, is celebrated with a table laid with seven things beginning with the letter s, and two days later Holi, the Hindu festival of colours. Easter comes early this year, in the last week of the month, and Purim and Eid al-Fitr fall in the same weeks.

The eagle and the wind of the east take over from the bee. At Vreta the equinox fire is lit in the ring of the winds, the sap is tapped from the birches and the Maya calendar’s new year, Wajxaqib’ B’atz’, is marked with the Evening of the Thread. It is a month for opening the windows and going out to listen.

intro: In March the sounds come back before the colours do. The great tit, the drip from the roof, the cranes calling far away. A listening walk is a walk where the ears go first.
steg: Go out early.
Ideally at dawn, when roads and people are quiet.
Walk slowly and quietly.
If there are several of you, agree not to talk until you are back.
Stop every hundred steps.
Close your eyes and count the sounds: one finger for every new sound.
Notice what is missing.
Which sound was not there in January?
Write when you get home.
A line about the first sound you heard and the last.

manader.ingress: In March everything wakes without promising anything. The sap rises in the birches, the cranes call over the fields and day and night grow equal.
stat: 13 h 15 min
of daylight on 31 March in Uppsala, against 10 h 32 min on 1 March. In a month the day grows by 2 h 43 min.
dates: The great night of Shiva. Hindus fast, keep vigil all night and pour milk, water and honey over Shiva’s lingam while mantras are sung.
International Women’s Day and new moon
A day for women’s rights, marked since the early twentieth century. The moon is new at 10.29.

8 B’atz’ in the Maya calendar, when the K’iche’ Maya’s sacred 260-day calendar is traditionally celebrated and new daykeepers are initiated. We are not daykeepers, but we let the day remind us of time as a thread that goes on being spun.
The festival marking the end of Ramadan, around these days depending on when the crescent moon is sighted. A day for prayer, shared meals and gifts.
Celebrated early this year, since Sunday 28 March is Easter Day. The old date of 25 March, Lady Day (vårfrudagen), has given us Waffle Day.
At 21.24 the sun crosses the celestial equator heading north, and spring begins astronomically. The sun rises almost due east and sets almost due west.

The Persian New Year, also celebrated by Kurds, Afghans and many peoples of Central Asia, is counted from the moment of the equinox. The haft-sin table is laid with seven things whose names begin with s, among them sprouted wheat.
Holy Week begins, in memory of Jesus’s entry into Jerusalem.
On the evening before Holi great fires are lit in memory of how the devout Prahlad was saved from the flames while the demoness Holika burned. Good triumphs over evil.
Full moon at 11.43. The same day Holi, the Hindu festival of colours, is celebrated, when people throw coloured powder at one another and leave winter behind.
The Jewish festival of joy in memory of the story in the Book of Esther. It begins the evening before, with dressing up, reading aloud and gifts of food.
The Easter witches (påskkärringar) go round with their Easter cards. It is also Waffle Day, the old Lady Day.
A public holiday and the quietest day in the Christian calendar.
Eggs, herring and Easter twigs. In Uppland the bonfires belong to Walpurgis Night, but in western Sweden Easter fires are lit tonight.
A public holiday and flag day. In the night before Sunday the clocks go forward an hour, from 02.00 to 03.00.
A public holiday. Then comes the Easter school holiday, week 13, up to and including Friday 2 April.
events: New moon at 10.29 and International Women’s Day. In the evening we write intentions for the spring and read aloud a poem by a woman, chosen by each person.

On 8 B’atz’ we gather in the sewing room for an evening with spinning wheel, weaving frame and mending. B’atz’ is the thread in the Maya calendar, and the evening is about time that goes on being spun. Tea and conversation, no ceremony.

We follow the sunset from the stone at the meadow’s edge and light the fire at the fire place. At 21.24, when the equinox occurs, there is a minute’s silence. Guests who celebrate Nowruz are welcome to lay their haft-sin table in the orangery.
Whoever celebrates the Persian New Year lays their table with the seven things in the orangery, and everyone is welcome to look and taste.
If the sap has begun to rise, we drill the first hole in one of the big birches and taste the sap at the long table. If it has not, we wait, and then the moon has to be enough.

The spirit hall stands open all day for anyone who wants to be in stillness, and a simple soup is made in the kitchen. Whoever keeps Good Friday as a Christian holy day does so, and whoever simply needs a quiet day has one.
An early morning walk in silence when we only listen. Afterwards we count together how many birds we heard.
We meet by the pond as the sun rises, just before half past six by the new summer time, and go on to Easter breakfast in the orangery. An egg hunt in the forest garden for the children.
fraga: What in me wants to wake now?
It need not be something new. It may be something that has slept a long time.
ord: Ñawi means eye but also bud – the place on a plant where something new is about to open. To open one’s ñawi is to let the new see the world. In March, when the buds swell, the word is close.
manader.hand: The sap knows when it is time.

manader.sub: The tipi is raised and winter is thanked
andetag: April is the month of saying yes. Everything that has lain still says yes at once: the frogs, the goat willow, the skylark, the nettles. In many traditions it is also the time of liberation and renewal. Passover tells of the exodus from slavery, Vaisakhi is the Sikh new year and harvest festival, and the Orthodox Church celebrates Easter only at the beginning of May.

At Vreta the tipi is raised in the meadow and becomes the spring’s ceremony room. The Frog Moon is celebrated in it, and the Walpurgis bonfire in the meadow is a thank-you to winter for the rest. It is also the month when we plant trees on Earth Day – the oldest form of hope there is.

intro: It is easy to be glad that winter is over. It is harder to thank it. Yet it gave something: rest, time, darkness to think in. A letter to winter is a way of seeing that.
steg: Write "Dear Winter".
At the top of a sheet of paper, by hand.
Write what it took.
What was hard, cold or long.
Write what it gave.
What could only happen in the darkness and the stillness.
Give thanks and say goodbye.
One sentence is enough.
Lay the letter in the fire.
On Walpurgis Night, in a bonfire or in a candle on the balcony.

manader.ingress: In April the pond wakes. The frogs sing at dusk, the tipi is raised in the meadow and winter is given its thanks at the Walpurgis bonfire.
stat: 15 h 57 min
of daylight on 30 April in Uppsala, against 13 h 21 min on 1 April. In a month the day grows by 2 h 36 min.
dates: New moon, Chaitra Navratri and Ugadi

The moon is new at 01.51. The Hindu spring festival Chaitra Navratri, nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga, begins and runs until 15 April. It ends with Ram Navami, Rama’s birthday. The same day Ugadi and Gudi Padwa, the new year in southern and western India, are celebrated.
The Sikh new year and harvest festival, in memory of the founding of the Khalsa in 1699. Celebrated this year around 14 April, often with processions and shared meals.
As it grows dark the waxing moon stands close to Jupiter and Mars high in the south-south-west – three lights in a small triangle.
Hindu festival for the birth of the god Rama, the last day of Chaitra Navratri. The Ramayana is read, and people fast and sing bhajans.
Full moon at 00.27 in the night before Wednesday. The moon stands low in the south all night.
Hindu festival for Hanuman, the monkey god who stands for loyalty, courage and strength. In northern India at the full moon in Chaitra.
The Jewish Passover, in memory of the exodus from Egypt, begins at sunset with the Seder meal and lasts seven or eight days. The first day is 22 April.
Marked since 1970, it gathers people all over the world around the earth and the climate. At Vreta we plant trees.
A meteor shower that has been observed for more than 2,500 years. This year the moon is almost full and washes out most of the shooting stars.

The great evening of spring. In Uppsala there is rafting down the Fyris river, the donning of student caps at 15.00 outside Carolina Rediviva and bonfires in the evening – this year during the university’s jubilee year. It is also the King’s birthday and a general flag day.
The Orthodox churches reckon Easter by the Julian calendar, and their Easter Day falls this year on 2 May.
events: When the ice has gone and the first mild evenings come, we gather by the pond to listen to the frogs singing. We use torches with red light, keep to the stones and lift nothing out of the water. Date depends on the weather.
New moon at 01.51. A short gathering by the pond at dusk, where the intentions are laid under stones by the water.
Anyone who celebrates the Sikh new year is welcome to share langar, the communal meal, at the long table.
We carry out the poles and the canvas and raise the tipi in the meadow together. Everyone who wants to help is welcome, and the day ends with soup and the first fire in the tipi’s hearth.
The Frog Moon in the tipi
The season’s first full moon ceremony in the tipi, with the fire in the middle and the door open towards the pond. The frogs sing outside, and the moon stands low in the south.
We plant bare-root trees and shrubs in the forest garden and along the meadow’s edge: apple, hazel, rowan and berry bushes. Each tree takes a wish with it into the ground. Open to all.
Songs from many traditions, always with a story of where they come from. Whoever does not want to sing may sit quietly.

Whoever wishes goes into Uppsala for the donning of the caps at 15.00. In the evening the Walpurgis bonfire is lit in the meadow, we sing in the spring and eat soup by the tipi. The bonfire is restacked the same day, so that no animals have had time to move in.
fraga: What do I want to say yes to this year?
Not to everything. To one thing, so clearly that it shows.
ord: Ayni is the foundation of Andean life: whoever receives gives back, between people and between people and nature. Whoever only takes breaks the balance. A k’intu is ayni in its smallest form.
manader.hand: Listen to the pond on an April evening.

andetag: May is the month of growing, and it is so full that it is easy to miss. The old gökotta – going out at dawn on Ascension Day to listen for the cuckoo – is a Swedish practice of attention older than most festivals. In the same month Vesak, the Buddha’s birth, awakening and death, is celebrated at the full moon, and Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, falls in the middle of Whitsun.

At Vreta the gökotta walk passes through the apple blossom in the forest garden. The Nettle Moon on 20 May coincides with Vesak, and we keep the evening in stillness by the pond. It is a month for walking barefoot, sleeping with the window open and letting the garden grow a little wilder than planned.

intro: The feet are the body’s most forgotten sense organ. In May, when the grass is soft and the dew lingers in the morning, it is easy to remind them of the ground.
steg: Go out early.
Before the dew has dried, ideally before anyone else is awake.
Take off your shoes.
Stand still for a while and feel the cold and the wet.
Walk slowly.
Notice the difference between grass, moss, gravel and soil.
Stop at a tree.
Lay your hand on the trunk. It is warmer than you think.
Dry your feet with your hands.
Not with a towel. That is part of the practice.

manader.ingress: In May everything wants to come up at once. The art is to find time to see it – and to let some of it be left in peace.
stat: 18 h 18 min
of daylight on 31 May in Uppsala, against 16 h 02 min on 1 May. In a month the day grows by 2 h 16 min.
dates: The day of the labour movement, a public holiday since 1939 and a general flag day. The same day the café and the shop open for the season.
The Celtic summer festival, midway between the spring equinox and midsummer. Fires were lit on the heights and the cattle driven between them for protection.
The Orthodox churches calculate Easter by the Julian calendar, and this year it falls five weeks after the Western one. Red-dyed eggs belong to the celebration.
A public holiday and the traditional day for gökotta – going out at dawn to listen to the birds, and with a little luck the cuckoo. The moon is new at 12.58.
One of the most auspicious days in Hinduism, when whatever is begun is said never to end. People give gifts, buy gold and start new projects.
On the evening of 12 May the waxing moon stands right beside Jupiter in the west-south-west. The next evening it has moved to Mars and Regulus, the brightest star in Leo.
By folk belief the last frost night of the year. No guarantee – but whoever waits until after Sophie with the frost-tender plants has seldom regretted it.
A public holiday and flag day. The Swedish name, pingst, comes from the Greek word for the fiftieth, and the festival falls on the fiftieth day counting from Easter Day.

The Festival of Sacrifice, one of the two great festivals of Islam, in memory of Ibrahim’s – Abraham’s – willingness to sacrifice. Celebrated with prayer, a shared meal and gifts to those in need. The exact date depends on when the crescent moon is seen.
The Buddha’s birth, enlightenment and passing are celebrated in many countries at the full moon in May. The moon is full at 12.58. The same day is the UN’s World Bee Day.
The UN’s international day for biodiversity. A good reason to count the species in the meadow, the pond and the forest garden.
events: We gather at the gate at 04.15, just before sunrise, and walk in silence through the forest garden to the meadow. There we listen, with flasks and blankets. Breakfast at the long table when the birds have finished singing.
New moon at 12.58 on the same day as the gökotta. In the evening we write intentions for the summer.
Anyone who celebrates Eid al-Adha is welcome to share the festive meal in the orangery. Whoever carries the tradition leads.

A quiet evening in the spirit hall with candles and meditation, ideally led by Buddhists from the area who wish to share their festival with us. Afterwards we walk down towards Ekoln to see whether the full moon shows as it rises low in the south-south-east.
On the International Day for Biological Diversity we open a path through the meadow that can only be walked barefoot. Grass, moss, sand, stone and clay.
A walk in silence to the old oak, now in full leaf-burst. We meet at the birch arch at 8.
fraga: What may grow wild in my life?
Not everything needs pruning. Some things should simply be allowed to come.
ord: The mountains are living beings in the Andes, apus, who watch over the valleys and the people. Ausangate is one of the mightiest. To greet an apu is to acknowledge that one is small, and that there is something that has stood longer than oneself.

andetag: June is the month of abundance. The light is so great it is almost hard to take in, and most cultures in the northern hemisphere have celebrated it with fire, flowers and dancing. Midsummer Eve (midsommarafton) is Sweden’s own solstice festival, with the maypole, flower crowns and seven kinds of flowers under the pillow. In Cusco Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the sun, is celebrated on 24 June – the same day as St John’s Day.

The grass snake and the wind of the south take over from the eagle. At Vreta we keep the night of the Bright Moon, the solstice evening and Midsummer in the meadow. The day after Midsummer Eve the Maya calendar’s round closes on 13 Ajpu, and on the Sunday a new one begins with 1 Imox – a round we mark with a while by the pond.

intro: In Swedish folk belief, whoever picks seven kinds of flowers in silence on Midsummer night and lays them under their pillow will dream of their future love. It is a game, but also a practice of attention: you have to see what is flowering and keep silent all the while.
steg: Go out after midnight.
Alone, or with someone who also promises to keep silent.
Pick seven kinds of flowers.
One of each, from the roadside or the meadow. Never protected species, and never more than you need.
Say nothing.
Not until the flowers are under the pillow.
Lay them under the pillow.
Notice the scent as you fall asleep.
Write in the morning.
What you dreamed, or what you thought about as you picked.

manader.ingress: In June the night never grows dark. The sun sets in the north-west and rises in the north-east, and in between lies only a blue dusk that never quite ends.
stat: 18 h 56 min
of daylight at the summer solstice on 21 June. The sun rises at 03.23 and sets at 22.19, and it never grows darker than a pale twilight.
dates: A public holiday and the day of the Swedish flag. Gustav Vasa was elected king on 6 June 1523, and on the same date in 1809 a new Instrument of Government was adopted.
Around this day the year 1449 after the Hijra begins, with the first crescent after the new moon on 4 June. The new year is usually marked quietly.
The Jewish Feast of Weeks, seven weeks after Passover, in memory of the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Begins at sunset the evening before. Dairy food and the year’s first fruits belong to it.
Sri Lankan Buddhist full moon day in memory of when the monk Mahinda brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka. Pilgrims climb the hill of Mihintale.
Full moon at 02.44, in the night between Friday and Saturday. The lowest full moon of the year – it reaches only a couple of degrees above the horizon in the south.
The sun turns at 16.10. The same day the Aymara people of the Andes celebrate their new year, Willkakuti – in the southern hemisphere it is the winter solstice, and the sun begins to return.
Inti Raymi and St John’s Day
The Inca festival of the sun, revived in Cusco since the mid-twentieth century. In the Christian calendar it is the day of John the Baptist – until 1953 also the Swedish Midsummer Day.

Not a public holiday in the legal sense, but the year’s greatest day of celebration for many Swedes. The maypole is dressed and raised, and the evening belongs to herring, new potatoes and strawberries.
A public holiday and flag day. In the Maya calendar it is 13 Ajpu, the last day of the sacred count of 260 days. Ajpu is often associated with the sun.
The Maya calendar’s count begins again with 1 Imox, a day associated with water. By folk belief, if it rains on Seven Sleepers’ Day it will rain for seven weeks.
events: New moon at 21.40. A short gathering by the pond in the light evening.
A day of stillness in the meadow
A day in silence outdoors, from 9 to 4, with sitting under the apple trees, walking along the stone wall and a wordless lunch.
The night of the Bright Moon

A night walk down towards Ekoln to try to see the full moon, which rises low in the south-south-east just before 23.00 and barely lifts above the treetops. We finish with the sauna and a while in silence by the pond.

When the sun turns at 16.10 we strike a single beat on one of the drums in the spirit hall. In the evening we gather in the meadow and follow the sun down in the north-west at 22.19, in silence. A small fire in the tipi if the fire risk allows.
On St John’s night we pick seven kinds of flowers in silence, as was done in Swedish folk belief, and lay them under the pillow.

In the morning we bind crowns and dress the maypole with birch twigs and meadow flowers. The pole is raised in the afternoon and we dance around it. Herring, new potatoes and strawberries at the long table under the oak, and late in the evening we walk through the woods down to the jetty on Ekoln. Booking in advance.

13 Ajpu and 1 Imox. An evening in the spirit hall about what has been completed, and an early morning by the pond about what is beginning. Inspired by the Maya calendar, with no claim to be anything else.
fraga: What have I been given more of than I need?
Abundance is not only having a lot. It is being able to give of it.
ord: Kawsay is everything that lives and the force that flows through it. Kawsay pacha, the living world, is the Andean name for the universe in which everything – mountain, water, stone and person – is alive and connected.
manader.hand: Stay up in the light for one night.

manader.sub: The scythe, the honey and the rest
andetag: July is the month when most people in Sweden are on holiday, and yet it is one of the hardest in which to be still. The light is long, the lists are long, and the holiday must be filled. But haymaking always had its pauses: the midday rest under the tree, the evening swim, the scythe being sharpened. In many traditions rest is sacred – the Sabbath, Sunday, Friday prayers – and it is here too.

At Vreta the meadow is cut with a scythe, and the bees have their day when the first honey is extracted. In old tradition people told the bees everything important, and we still do. The Haymaking Moon on 18 July is celebrated with a long table under the open sky.

intro: Resting is not doing nothing. It is doing nothing on purpose. An hour in July without phone, book or company is more than most of us give ourselves in a year.
steg: Choose an hour.
Ideally in the middle of the day or in the evening light.
Lie down outdoors.
In the grass, in a hammock or on a blanket under a tree.
Leave everything else.
Phone indoors, book indoors.
Look at the sky.
The clouds, the leaves, the birds. Let your gaze wander without stopping.
Get up when the hour is over.
Not before, even if it feels long.

manader.ingress: July is fullness. Everything has grown, nothing has yet begun to wither, and in the middle of it stands the hardest practice of all: to rest.
stat: 17 h 00 min
of daylight on 31 July in Uppsala, against 18 h 47 min on 1 July. In a month the day shrinks by 1 h 48 min.
dates: The moon is new at 05.01. The Haymaking Moon’s round begins, but on the first evenings the crescent is too thin and too low to be seen in the light sky.
Around now the earth begins to pass through the Perseid meteor stream. So far there are only occasional shooting stars in the light nights – the maximum comes on the night of 12–13 August.
Full moon at 17.44. A very faint penumbral eclipse occurs around 18.00, before the moon has risen here. The moon rises just after sunset, around 22.00.

The same full moon carries two festivals. Hindus, Buddhists and Jains thank their teachers on Guru Purnima, and Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha’s first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath, when the wheel of the teaching was set in motion.
The rains retreat begins for Theravada monks, who stay in their monasteries for three months. Many lay people give something up during the same time.

By folk belief they last until 23 August, a time when food spoils and wounds heal badly. They are also called the dog days after Sirius, the Dog Star, which in antiquity rose with the sun at this time.
The feast of St Bridget of Sweden. She was Sweden’s first saint and one of the patron saints of Europe, and her revelations were written down in Vadstena.
"St James drops a cold stone in the lake." The water is said to begin cooling now. At Vreta the last stretches of the meadow are cut, and the day ends with a haymaking feast.
The moon wanes and leaves the darkening nights to the stars. The Summer Triangle – Vega, Deneb and Altair – stands high in the south around midnight.
In memory of Olaf the Holy, who fell at Stiklestad in 1030. In Norway the day is called Olsok, and in the Faroe Islands Ólavsøka is the national day.
events: New moon at 05.01. A morning moment by the pond before breakfast.
A Sunday with no programme. The hammocks hang under the apple trees, the coffee is out and nobody needs to do anything.

We show how a frame is uncapped and extracted in a closed room the bees cannot reach, taste honey straight from the comb and talk about varroa and the wild bees. The new honey is sold in the shop the same day.
Long table under the Haymaking Moon

A slow dinner of July’s harvest under the apple tree, with lanterns on the table. When the moon rises in the south-east around 22.00 we walk a little way into the meadow and watch it lift above the trees.
Drum journey under the open sky
An evening with the frame drum in the meadow, lying on blankets as dusk comes.
The darkness has begun to come back, and for the first time since May the lanterns are needed. Tales and stories for children and adults in the tipi, with sheepskins on the floor.
fraga: What do I not need to do?
The list of what must be done is always long. The list of what need not be done is often longer.
ord: Yachay is one of the three Andean forces, the knowledge that comes from experience. It belongs with munay, love, and llankay, work. Without love wisdom grows cold, and without work it becomes mere words.
manader.hand: Rest in the midst of what grows.

andetag: August is the month of ripening. The berries ripen, the apples colour and the first morning mist settles over the pond. In the Celtic tradition 1 August is Lughnasadh, the first harvest festival, when the first bread was baked from the year’s grain. In the Andes August is Pachamama’s month, when the earth is given back something of what it has given.

At Vreta we thank the earth on 1 August and watch the partial solar eclipse on 2 August projected on a linen cloth. The Perseids reach their maximum on the night of 13 August, and it is the best night of the year for lying in the grass and looking up. It is a month for harvesting, and for seeing how small one is.

intro: Lying under a starry sky is one of the oldest spiritual practices there is, and it asks nothing. The light from many of the stars has been on its way for hundreds of years. Knowing that does something to time.
steg: Choose a clear night.
Ideally the night of 13 August, for the Perseids.
Go away from the light.
Let your eyes adjust for twenty minutes.
Lie down.
On a blanket, with your head towards the north-east.
Do not count the shooting stars.
Let them come.
Think of someone who has seen the same sky.
Long before you, or far away.

manader.ingress: In August the darkness comes back, and with it the stars. What has grown all summer turns sweet, and the evenings gain a seriousness they lacked in July.
stat: 14 h 19 min
of daylight on 31 August in Uppsala, against 16 h 55 min on 1 August. In a month the day shrinks by 2 h 35 min.
dates: In the Andes August is counted as the month of Pachamama, Mother Earth. It is then customary to give back to the earth – food, drink and thanks – before a new growing season. We invite those who carry the tradition, but we do not take it over.
The Celtic first harvest festival, when the first bread was baked from the year’s grain. In England called Lammas, the loaf mass.
Between about 10.39 and 12.00 the moon covers a small part of the sun, at most around 11.19. In Spain, North Africa and Egypt the eclipse is total. Never look directly at the sun.
At 12.05, the same morning as the eclipse. It is the new moon that makes the eclipse possible – the moon then stands between the earth and the sun.
The most reliable meteor shower of the year. The moon sets at 23.30, and after midnight the sky is dark until dawn at around 03.30.
Japanese Buddhist festival when the ancestors are said to come home. Graves are tidied, lanterns lit and bon-odori danced. On the last evening lanterns are set out on the water.
The Prophet Muhammad’s birthday is celebrated by many Muslims around 15 August, from the night of the 14th. The date follows the lunar calendar and may differ by a day.
The Hungry Ghost Festival in China and Vietnam, the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month. Food is offered, incense burned and lanterns set out for the dead.
Full moon at 09.28. The moon rises just after 20.00 both the evening before and the evening after and runs low across the southern sky all night.
Hindu festival of the bond between siblings. Sisters tie a thread, a rakhi, round their brother’s wrist, and the brother promises to protect her.
In folk belief the dog days were reckoned from 23 July to 23 August – a time when food was thought to spoil quickly and the flies were many. Even so, it is now that we make jam.
Krishna’s birth is celebrated at midnight with fasting, song and games. In Maharashtra young people form towers to reach a pot of butter.
The month’s second new moon, at 19.41. The evening is dark, and the late-summer starry sky stands clear once the twilight has passed.
events: A morning moment in the forest garden when we give back: compost under the apple trees, water for the young trees and a while in silence by the old oak. Whoever carries the Andean tradition is welcome to hold their own ceremony here.
At Lughnasadh a loaf is baked in the wood oven from flour from a neighbouring farm. The first bread broken is left for the birds.
From 10.30 under the birches by the meadow. We lend approved eclipse glasses, build pinhole cameras from cardboard and follow the crescents on a white cloth. For all ages.
We put out the lanterns at midnight and lay out sleeping mats and blankets in the meadow. Hot drinks at the fire place if the fire risk allows. Whoever wishes may sleep on in the tipi.
Full moon at 09.28. In the evening we sit by the pond as the moon rises, with a bowl of berries from the forest garden.
New moon at 19.41, the second in August. An intention for the autumn is written by the light of the first lantern.
fraga: What has ripened in me since spring?
What has ripened is not always visible. Sometimes it only feels as though something has turned sweet.
ord: Pacha means the earth and the world, but also time. Pachamama is thus both the earth we stand on and the time we live in. Whoever gives to her gives back to what carries them.
manader.hand: Look up. It has always been there.

manader.sub: Equinox, thanks and the passage of the cranes
andetag: September is the month of thanks. Harvest festivals exist in every culture that has grown food, and they are surprisingly alike: a table, food from the earth, thanks to what has given. In China and Vietnam the Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated at the full moon with mooncakes and lanterns. The International Day of Peace on 21 September is a day for silence at noon, and the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, comes at the beginning of October.

The bear and the wind of the west take over from the grass snake. At Vreta the Harvest Moon is celebrated by the pond, the autumn equinox with a dawn in the ring of the winds and the harvest festival at the long table in the meadow. It is a month for giving thanks, and for beginning to prepare the rest.

intro: A word of thanks before food exists in almost every tradition, and it need not be addressed to anyone in particular. It can be addressed to the hands that have carried the food all the way to the table.
steg: Wait before you eat.
Everyone is seated, the food is on the table.
Look at the food.
Where does it come from? A field, a forest, a sea, a greenhouse.
Think of the hands.
Those who have sown, harvested, driven, sold and cooked.
Say thank you.
Aloud or silently, in your own words or with a word from your tradition.
Eat the first mouthful slowly.
Taste it.

manader.ingress: In September the harvest is brought in. Day and night grow equal again, the cranes call over the meadow and the long table is laid for everyone.
stat: 11 h 39 min
of daylight on 30 September in Uppsala, against 14 h 14 min on 1 September. In a month the day shrinks by 2 h 35 min.
dates: Hindu festival for Ganesha, the elephant god who removes obstacles. Clay figures of Ganesha are worshipped in homes and streets for up to ten days and then immersed in water.
Kerala’s great harvest festival, in memory of the good king Mahabali who visits his people every year. Flower carpets, boat races and a feast on banana leaves.

In China and much of East Asia the moon festival is celebrated at the full moon of the eighth lunar month, this year on the evening of 15 September. Families gather, look at the moon and share mooncakes.
Full moon at 01.03 in the night before Thursday. On Wednesday evening the moon rises around 18.37, a good half hour before the sun sets.
The UN’s day of peace, when the world is urged to observe a day of ceasefire and non-violence. A day close to Vreta’s outlook.
At 08.01 the sun crosses the celestial equator heading south. The sun rises at 06.33 almost due east and sets at 18.49 almost due west.
At 12.20, the same day as the equinox. The moon is half light and half dark – like the day.
Michaelmas was one of the great boundaries of the farming year. The harvest was to be in, and the old year of service drew to its end.
At 04.35. The darkest nights of the month, good for stars and, if the sun is active, for the northern lights low in the north.
The Hindu nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga begin on 30 September and continue into October. The festival is celebrated differently in different regions, often with fasting, song and dance.
events: The Harvest Moon by the pond

We gather by the pond just before 18.37 and watch the moon rise in the east while the sun has not yet set. Anyone who celebrates the Mid-Autumn Festival is welcome to bring mooncakes and tell us about it.
On the evening of the Mid-Autumn Festival we hang paper lanterns in the apple tree and share mooncakes from the café.
On the International Day of Peace the bell by the cottage rings at noon. Whoever is on the place stops for a minute in silence.
At sunrise at 06.33 we stand at the fire place in the meadow and mark where the sun rises. Porridge and coffee in the orangery when the equinox occurs at 08.01.

The year’s biggest celebration. The long table is laid in the meadow with bread from the wood oven, soup from the harvest and juice from the press, for neighbours, guests and everyone who has helped during the year. With a little luck the cranes pass over us.

We go through the year’s growing notes in the orangery and enter the harvest in the site journal: what grew, what failed and what we will do differently next year. The seed packets are labelled and sorted.
New moon at 04.35. An intention for the autumn, written by candlelight in the spirit hall in the evening.
fraga: Who carries me without my seeing it?
There are always more hands behind something than you think.
ord: Llankay is the third force, that of action and work. In the Andes work is not something you do in order to escape, but a way of being in the world. The harvest is llankay that has been allowed to bear fruit.

manader.sub: Leaf fall, light and letting go
andetag: October is the month of farewells. It is hard to watch a tree let go of its leaves without thinking of what you yourself are holding on to. In the same month come the Jewish festivals of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkot, with new year, atonement and leaf huts, and Diwali, the Hindu festival of light, when lamps are lit along roads and in windows to show the light the way home.

At Vreta the Mushroom Moon is celebrated on 15 October, and clay lamps are shaped in the ceramics workshop ahead of Diwali. The tipi’s last fire burns before the canvas is taken down for the winter. On 31 October the clocks go back an hour, and the same evening is Samhain, the old Celtic new year’s night, when the boundary between the living and the dead was said to be at its thinnest.

intro: A tree lets go of its leaves to survive the winter. It is not a loss, but a preparation. The practice is to do the same with something you are holding on to for longer than you need.
steg: Go out among the trees.
On a day when the leaves are falling.
Pick a leaf for each thing.
Something you want to stop doing, a thought that has grown too tight, a grudge.
Hold the leaves in your hand.
Say quietly what each one stands for.
Lay them on the ground.
Or in the compost, where they become soil.
Go home without them.
Notice how your hands feel.

manader.ingress: In October the trees let go of their leaves without hesitating. What has been finished for weeks falls to the ground and becomes soil.
stat: 8 h 55 min
of daylight on 31 October in Uppsala, against 11 h 33 min on 1 October. In a month the day shrinks by 2 h 39 min.
dates: The Jewish New Year 5788 begins at sunset. The shofar is blown, and apple dipped in honey is eaten for a sweet new year.
The eighth day of Navratri, the high point of Durga Puja in Bengal, where the goddess Durga is honoured for her victory over the demon Mahishasura.
The tenth day, Vijayadashami: Rama’s victory over Ravana and Durga’s victory over the demon. Giant figures of Ravana are burned, and good triumphs over evil.
The Church of Sweden’s thanksgiving service for the harvest. Many churches are decorated with bread, fruit and vegetables from the district.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, with fasting and prayer. It begins at sunset the evening before.
Full moon at 15.46. The moon rises in the east-north-east just before 17.00, before the sun has set.
The Theravada monks’ rains retreat ends with Pavarana, when the monks ask one another for forgiveness. The same full moon as the Mushroom Moon.
The Feast of Tabernacles begins the evening before and lasts seven days. Meals are eaten in a hut roofed with branches, sparse enough to see the stars. It too is a harvest festival.
The Buddhist month of the robe offering: lay people give new robes and provisions to the monasteries after the rains retreat.
Shooting stars from dust left behind by Halley’s Comet. The moon is almost half and interferes, but the odd fast meteor may be seen after midnight.
A flag day. The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.
The first day of Diwali. Something new of metal is bought and the first lamp lit for health and prosperity.
The festival of light is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, this year on the same day as the new moon, at 15.36. Clay lamps are lit in windows and along paths – light over darkness.
The day after Diwali, Krishna, who lifted the mountain Govardhan to shelter the farmers, is honoured with mountains of food that are shared out.
The last day of Diwali, when sisters pray for their brothers and the brothers give gifts.
The clocks go back an hour at 03.00. The mornings grow lighter, and the sun sets as early as 15.59.
Pumpkin lanterns and children in costume. The Swedish All Saints’ weekend (allhelgonahelgen) comes the weekend after, on 5–6 November.
The Celtic new year’s night, when summer ended and winter began. The boundary between the living and the dead was said to be at its thinnest.
events: A soul walk through the broadleaf woods in silence, when each person picks a leaf for something to be let go.

On Harvest Thanksgiving we lay the long table in the orangery with the year’s harvest. Each person brings something they have grown, picked or made and tells what they want to give thanks for. The season’s first fire is lit in the fireplace.
We watch the moon rise just before 17.00 as the sun sets. Mushroom soup at the fire place and a short walk in the moonlight down to the pond.
Clay lamps in the ceramics workshop
We shape small lamps of clay, let them dry and fire them in the kiln. Whoever celebrates Diwali gets lamps for their festival, and whoever does not gets light for the November dark.
During Sukkot we build a simple leaf hut by the stone wall, and anyone who celebrates is welcome to eat their meals there.

On Friday evening we light a last fire in the tipi and give thanks for the season. On Saturday it is taken down among the yellow birches: the canvas is dried and folded, the poles carried in and its place in the meadow raked.

If those who celebrate wish, clay lamps are lit along the stone path and on the granite boulders by the pond. Those who carry the tradition lead the evening. The rest of us help, listen and light a lamp if asked.
fraga: What am I holding on to that is already finished?
A leaf that clings on in winter does no good. It only catches snow.
ord: Hucha is energy that has grown heavy because it has not been allowed to move – grief, anger, worry. It is not dangerous and not evil. It only needs to come back to the earth, where it becomes nourishment again.

andetag: November is the month of memory. The All Saints’ weekend, with candles on the graves, is one of the few Swedish festivals that almost everyone keeps, whatever their faith. In Mexico Día de Muertos is celebrated with altars, marigolds and the favourite foods of the dead, and many Asian traditions have days for the ancestors through the year. It is as though the darkness itself reminds us of those who are no longer in the light.

At Vreta candles are lit along the stone wall on All Saints’ Eve, and the Day of Remembrance in the spirit hall gives room to everyone who wants to remember someone. The Dark Moon on 14 November covers the Pleiades. The Maya calendar’s new year, Wajxaqib’ B’atz’, comes a second time on 24 November, and the month ends in waiting – with the first Sunday of Advent and a new moon on the same day.

ovning.titel: The letter to one who has gone before
intro: There are things you did not have time to say, and things you would like to tell. A letter to someone who has died is not a way of getting an answer, but a way of giving the words a place.
steg: Light a candle.
Ideally on All Saints’ Eve, or on a day that means something to the two of you.
Write the person’s name at the top.
By hand.
Tell what has happened.
In your life, in the world, in the garden.
Write what you did not have time to say.
Or what you want to say again.
Keep the letter or leave it.
In a book, under a stone or in the fire.

manader.ingress: In November it gets truly dark. It is the month when most cultures have honoured their dead, and when the candles in the churchyards can be seen further than at any time of year.
stat: 6 h 41 min
of daylight on 30 November in Uppsala, against 8 h 50 min on 1 November. In a month the day shrinks by 2 h 09 min.
dates: The Days of the Dead in Mexico. The family builds an altar with marigolds, candles, photographs and the favourite foods of the dead, and visits the graves.
Hindu festival for the sun in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. People fast, stand in the river and make offerings to the setting sun and, the next morning, to the rising sun.
The sun sets around 15.45. At dusk we light the candles along the stone wall and by the pond.
A public holiday and a day for remembering those who have gone before us. Many light candles on graves and in memorial groves.
A flag day in memory of the king who fell at Lützen in 1632. The pastry of the day bears his profile in chocolate or marzipan.
Goose dinner, above all a tradition from Skåne. It is linked both to Martin of Tours, whose day is 11 November, and to Martin Luther, who was born on 10 November 1483.
Father’s Day and the Dark Moon
The second Sunday in November. The moon is full at 04.25 and stands in the west, while Jupiter shines in the south-east.
Kartik Purnima and Guru Nanak’s birthday
The full moon of Kartik. Hindus bathe in sacred rivers and light thousands of lamps along the Ganges in Varanasi, and Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak’s birth with processions and langar.
A meteor shower with a dramatic history. This year a waning but almost full moon shines for most of the night, and most of the shooting stars are drowned in its glow.
The Sunday of the Last Judgement
The last Sunday of the church year. The same night, at 01.48, the moon is at last quarter.
8 B’atz’ in the K’iche’ count of days, 260 days after 9 March. B’atz’ is the thread from which time is spun. We are inspired, not daykeepers.
First Sunday of Advent and new moon
The first candle is lit. The moon is new at 04.24, and the evening of Advent Sunday is the darkest of the month.
events: During the Days of the Dead an altar with marigolds and candles stands in the orangery. Anyone may place a photograph or a name there.
At dusk we light lanterns along the stone wall and on the granite boulders by the pond. Whoever wishes writes a name and lays it by a candle. Open to all, in silence.
The Day of Remembrance in the spirit hall
The hall stands open from dawn to dusk with candles and a book in which names can be written. No ceremony – each person comes and goes. The café is open with Gustavus Adolphus pastries.
The Dark Moon morning and Father’s Day
We walk to the pond in the dark and watch the full moon sink in the west. Then breakfast in the orangery and a fired sauna in the afternoon.
An evening with the frame drum in the spirit hall. The drum beats a steady rhythm, and each person lies with a question about what has been.
On 8 B’atz’ we gather in the sewing room to spin, weave bands and mend. We tell of the K’iche’ count of days as inspiration, not as ceremony.
The new moon’s intention and the first Sunday of Advent
New moon at 04.24. The first Advent candle is lit in the cottage, and each person writes an intention for the winter.
fraga: Whom do I carry with me?
Those who have gone before remain in how we do things, in songs we know and in trees they planted.
ord: Ayllu is the Andean community, the kin and the village – but also the dead, the mountains and the earth that belong to it. Nobody is alone in an ayllu. Those who have gone before are still part of it.
manader.hand: Light a candle for the one you miss.

manader.sub: Lucia at the full moon and the second turning of the sun
andetag: The second December in the book is not like the first. A round has passed, and what was waiting last year is now also memory. This year St Lucia’s Day coincides with the full moon, so the Lucia procession walks in the light of both candles and moon. Hanukkah begins on Christmas Eve, and the two festivals of light shine in the same window all through Christmas week.

At Vreta Bodhi Day is kept in stillness, St Lucia’s Day at the full moon and the winter solstice with a vigil in the meadow. The bee and the wind of the north are back. It is a month for looking back on what has been and gathering what is to be carried on.

intro: Keeping vigil on the longest night is one of the oldest ceremonies there is. You need not stay up all night. It is enough to stay up later than usual, and to see the dawn when it comes.
steg: Choose the night.
The night before 22 December, or another of the longest nights.
Light a candle at sunset.
At 14.48. Let it burn all evening.
Fill the night slowly.
Read, tell stories, cook, sit in silence. Do what you never otherwise have time for.
Rest when you need to.
The vigil is not an ordeal.
See the dawn.
Go out when the sky lightens in the south-east, and see the first day with longer light.

manader.ingress: December again, a round later. The darkness is the same, but whoever has followed the year now knows that it turns.
stat: 6 h 02 min
of daylight at the winter solstice on 22 December. A year after the last solstice the day is exactly as long – it is we who have changed.
dates: Two candles burn. The café and the shop have Advent opening.
In Zen Buddhist tradition, among others, the day of the Buddha’s awakening under the bodhi tree. The spirit hall stands open for anyone who wants to sit in stillness.
Hindu festival for the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna’s teaching to Arjuna. The Gita is read and recited.
The day after the Christmas market. Three candles burn, and the café has Advent opening.
St Lucia’s Day and the Winter Moon
Full moon at 17.08. "Lucia – the long night of Lusse": in the old Julian calendar St Lucia’s Day lay close to the longest night of the year.
In an ordinary year the richest meteor shower. This year the moon is almost full and shines all night, so only the brightest shooting stars show.
All four candles burn. The last Advent weekend with the café open.
"Thomas with the barrel" in the old calendar – the Christmas ale was to be ready. The night that follows is the longest of the year.
The UN’s day for meditation, established in 2024 and marked at the winter solstice. A day to sit still, wherever you are.
The sun turns at 03.41. The autumn term ends the same day.
The day when most of Christmas is celebrated in Sweden, with the tree, the Christmas smorgasbord (julbord) and presents.
The Jewish festival of light begins at sunset on Christmas Eve and lasts eight days. Each evening one more candle is lit in the hanukkiah.
Two public holidays. Christmas Day is also a flag day, and in many churches the early Christmas service, julotta, is held early in the morning.
The last evening of the year. We meet it by the fire, not with bangers.
events: An hour in the still room on the second Sunday of Advent: a candle, a song and silence.
From sunrise at 08.32 to sunset at 14.50 the spirit hall stands open for silent sitting. Come and go at your own pace. Tea in the orangery afterwards.

The Lucia procession sets off at 17.00 from the farmhouse through the garden, past the orangery and down to the pond, while the Winter Moon rises over the birches. Battery candles in the crowns. Saffron buns and glögg in the orangery afterwards.
The last walk in silence of the year, to the old oak in the snow. Each person carries a question about the year that has passed.

At sunset we light a small fire at the fire place in the meadow, within a ring of lanterns. We keep watch in shifts through the longest night of the year and stand in silence for a while at 03.41. Breakfast in the orangery when the sun rises at 08.47.
The orangery’s windows and long table are available to anyone who wishes to light the hanukkiah. We provide the room and latkes, and those who carry the festival decide how it is celebrated.
New moon at 21.12, between Christmas and New Year. An intention for the new year is written by the candlelight in the cottage.
New Year’s Eve by the fire

The year’s last sauna and a quick dip in the ice hole, then a fire at the fire place and the year’s last page in the site journal. No fireworks – for the sake of the hens, the wild animals and the neighbours’ animals.
fraga: What have I learned from the darkness this year?
The darkness is the same as last year. The question is whether you see it differently.
ord: Pachakuti means roughly that time and the world are turned over. In Andean thought such upheavals come in cycles, when one time ends and a new one begins. A pachakuti can be large or small, for the world or for a single person.

manader.sub: The eclipse at dawn and the year book
andetag: A year is a breath, and January 2028 is the out-breath. On 12 January the Ice Moon is slightly eclipsed at dawn, with a small dark notch in its edge as it stands low in the west. On 26 January it is Chinese New Year, the Year of the Monkey, at the same time as an annular solar eclipse on the other side of the world. Shortly afterwards Ramadan begins.

At Vreta the year book is read at the oak table, and whoever has written in this book can do the same. It is not to judge what has been, but to see it. What has taken root may grow on. What did not may become soil.

intro: If you have written in the book’s pages during the year, you now have a year book. Reading it aloud, to yourself or to someone else, is a way of seeing a year all at once.
steg: Choose an evening.
Ideally at the full moon on 12 January or the new moon on the 26th.
Light a candle.
The same kind of light as last December.
Read from the beginning.
The intentions and the thanks, month by month.
Underline what took root.
What really grew, even if it did not turn out as you planned.
Write a sentence for the new round.
At the top of an empty page.

manader.ingress: January again, and a round has closed. It is time to read what you wrote and see what took root.
stat: 8 h 00 min
of daylight on 31 January in Uppsala, against 6 h 11 min on 1 January. In a month the day grows by 1 h 48 min.
dates: A public holiday and flag day. In the K’iche’ count of days it is 7 Toj, a day usually associated with the offering – giving back for what one has received.
The moon sets around 23.20. After midnight and towards dawn the sky is dark enough for shooting stars.
A public holiday. The last holy day of Christmas, in memory of the wise men who followed the star.
Celebrated by the Orthodox churches that keep to the Julian calendar.
The Ice Moon and a lunar eclipse
Full moon at 05.02 and a small partial eclipse, greatest around 05.13, with the moon in the west. The same day the spring term begins.
Christmas is danced out and the tree carried out. The old year is truly over.
The Night of Forgiveness in the Islamic calendar, two weeks before Ramadan. The night is often spent in prayer and in memory of the dead. The date is approximate.
A Punjabi winter fire with sesame, peanuts and dancing round the bonfire.
Hindu harvest festival when the sun enters Capricorn. Kites are flown and sesame sweets shared.
New moon and Chinese New Year
New moon at 16.12. The same day the Chinese New Year begins, the Year of the Monkey.
International day of remembrance on the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz in 1945. We light a candle in the spirit hall.
The Islamic month of fasting begins when the new moon’s crescent is seen, around 27–28 January. The fast lasts from dawn to sunset.
Hindu spring festival for Saraswati, goddess of knowledge and music, celebrated in yellow clothes. Some calendars give 1 February.
events: As a year ago: a walk along the shore of Ekoln to the old oak, without words, and breakfast in the orangery.
The Quadrantids from the meadow once the moon has set. We warm up in the sauna first and lie down on skins and sleeping mats after midnight.
The year book at the oak table

Two days when the year’s notes, photographs and finds are read through together, one month at a time. For everyone who has been part of the year: guests, course participants, volunteers and neighbours.
We gather by the pond at 04.30 with lanterns and binoculars and watch the umbra nip the edge of the moon. Head torches and ice picks, but we stay on land. Breakfast in the orangery as it grows light.
The Christmas tree back to the woods
The Christmas tree from our own thinning is carried back to the woodland edge and becomes a brush pile, shelter for small birds and small animals. So a round closes.
A day in silence from 9 to 4, with sitting, walking and a simple wordless lunch.
The new moon’s intention and new year
New moon at 16.12 and Chinese New Year. An intention for the new round, and dumplings in the café.
fraga: What took root, and what became soil?
Both belong. What became soil makes next year more fertile.
ord: Munay means to love and to will at the same time – a love that chooses. It is the first of the three forces and the one the others rest on. It is also the first part of the name Munay-Ki, the energy of love.
manader.hand: One round. We begin again where we stand.

manader.sub: Candlemas, Ramadan and the leap day
andetag: The last month in the book is a month of light. Candlemas and the Sámi National Day fall on the same Sunday, 6 February, and the New Year of the Trees, Tu Bishvat, is celebrated once the Light Moon has been full. Ramadan lasts the whole month and ends with Eid al-Fitr in the last days of the month. Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, is kept on 23 February with vigil and fasting.

And then it is a leap year. 29 February is a day that comes only every fourth year, a day that does not quite belong to the calendar. At Vreta we give it away: no plans, no musts, just a day to receive. That is where this book leaves you.

intro: Every fourth year we are given a day that does not quite belong to the calendar. It is an addition, an adjustment because the solar year does not divide evenly into days. The practice is to receive it as a gift and not fill it.
steg: Plan nothing.
Let 29 February stay empty in the calendar.
Begin with the light.
Watch the sunrise at 06.47, from a window or a door.
Do one thing you never have time for.
Just one. Let the rest of the day stay open.
Give something away.
Time, a thought, something you have made with your hands.
Write the last page.
In this book, or in a new one.

manader.ingress: Every festival in the calendar carries a story. Here they are gathered tradition by tradition: what they stand for, how they are expressed and what they symbolise.
stat: 10 h 31 min
of daylight on leap day, 29 February, in Uppsala, against 8 h 05 min on 1 February. The sun rises at 06.47 and sets at 17.17.
dates: The Celtic spring festival, midway between the winter solstice and the spring equinox. Candles are lit for Brigid.
At 20.10. The moon grows towards the Light Moon.
The Sámi winter market, held in Jokkmokk since 1605.
Candlemas Day and Sámi National Day
Candlemas, the mass of light, falls on the same Sunday as the Sámi National Day, when the flag of Sápmi is raised and the national anthem sung.
Tamil festival for Murugan at the full moon in Thai, with pilgrims carrying kavadi.
Full moon at 16.03. It rises in the north-east at dusk and shines over the snow all night.
The Theravada Buddhists’ Sangha Day at the Light Moon, with a candle procession round the temple.
The New Year of the Trees in the Jewish calendar, from sunset on 11 February. Fruits from the land’s trees are eaten and new ones planted.
St Valentine’s Day, in Sweden mostly a day for friendship and kindness.
Day of remembrance for the Buddha’s passing and final liberation.
The Night of Power, when by tradition the first verses of the Qur’an were revealed. Kept on one of the last odd nights of Ramadan, usually the 27th. The date is approximate.
The great night of Shiva, with fasting, vigil and prayer. One of the most important nights in Hinduism.
The feast of the Apostle Matthias. "Matthias breaks the ice; if there is no ice, he makes ice."
At 11.37. The last new moon in the book.
The festival of breaking the fast when Ramadan ends, depending on when the new moon’s crescent is seen. A day for prayer, gifts and food together.
The Tibetan New Year, with cleansing, prayers and fifteen days of festivities.
A day that comes only every fourth year, and on the same day Shrove Tuesday. Ash Wednesday and Lent begin the day after.
events: A straw cross is plaited in the cottage at Imbolc, and a plate of bread and milk is set in the window.
New beeswax candles are dipped in the workshop from the wax of the place’s hives, and the first are lit in the evening. The same day the flag of Sápmi is raised by the cottage.
An evening in the spirit hall as the Light Moon rises. Each person reads an intention from the book’s first month and sees what has become of it.
The New Year of the Trees
On Tu Bishvat we walk a round of the forest garden and stop for a while at each fruit tree. Dried fruit and nuts in the café afterwards.
Anyone fasting during Ramadan is welcome to break the fast at the long table in the orangery. The sun sets at 16.52. Whoever carries the tradition leads the evening.
The book’s last new moon. An intention for what comes after the book is written and laid under a stone on the altar.
A day with no programme, open to all. The coffee is out, the fire burns in the meadow and whoever wishes can read aloud from their year book. Semlor in the café.
fraga: What do I do with time I had not counted on?
The extra day is a question mark in the calendar. The answer is yours.
ord: Sumaq kawsay means the good, beautiful life – a life in balance with other people and with nature, where one has enough and no more. The concept has been written into the constitutions of Ecuador and Bolivia. It is perhaps the best summary of what this book tries to say.

manar: Turning. The darkness is deepest, and the light turns.
Stillness. What rests should be allowed to rest.
Waiting. The light comes before the warmth.
Waking. The sap rises and the windows are opened.
Saying yes. Winter is thanked and the fire is lit.
Growing. Everything wants to come up at once.
Abundance. The night never grows dark.
Fullness. Rest in the midst of what grows.
Ripening. What has grown turns sweet.
Thanks. The harvest is brought in and shared.
Farewell. What is finished is let go.
Memory. Those who have gone before are given a candle.
Turning. A round closes at the solstice.
Return. The moon is slightly eclipsed at dawn.
The light first. The book leaves you here.
delar: To create with patience and live on what those who came before us have gathered.
To rise, see the whole and dare to see what does not yet exist.
To shed the skin and let go of what has grown too tight.
To walk through the dark instead of fleeing it, and to see rest as part of transformation.
To remember, gather and begin again with what one has.
stunder: Before the phone: a window, three breaths and a question – what do I want to pay attention to today?
Before the food: a thought for the hands that grew, carried and cooked it. Aloud, if there are several of you.
Before sleep: thanks for one thing that happened today, however small. Put out the light with it.
sa_anvands: Each day has its Maya day, the phase of the moon and the festivals that fall on it. Public holidays and flag days are marked, as is what happens at Vreta.
Festivals from many traditions, with a short explanation. Dates that follow the moon or another calendar may shift by a day depending on where one is.
The place’s ceremonies and gatherings. Those that also appear in *The Calendar Year* have the same dates there.
Something simple to do alone or with a few others, at home or outdoors. No experience needed.
A question for the month. It needs no answer – it only needs to come along.

A rite from the Andes – from Munay-Ki, a contemporary series of rites from The Four Winds Society inspired by Andean traditions, or from the rituals of the Q’ero people, which we describe but do not perform without an invitation – and a word of wisdom in Quechua to carry with you.
The new moon’s intention and the full moon’s thanks. After fifteen months you have a year book of your own.
andras: Learn what the festival is about and when it falls. The Jewish and the Islamic day begin at sunset the evening before.
If you want to mark someone else’s festival, ask how. A "Happy Christmas", an "Eid Mubarak" or a "Chag Sameach" is almost always welcome.
Let whoever carries the tradition lead.
At Vreta a festival is led by those who celebrate it. The place lends the room, the food is adapted and whoever wishes to pray is given a quiet place.
What belongs to a group we leave there. We do not joik, we burn no white sage and we hold no ceremonies that require an initiation we do not have.
andras_p: The book includes festivals from traditions that are not Vreta’s own.
