It is not to borrow them, but to know when a neighbour is fasting, when a colleague celebrates new year and when a friend lights candles. Often it is enough to know. Sometimes one is invited. At the back of the book all the festivals are described, tradition by tradition: what they stand for, how they are celebrated and what they symbolise.
hallning: Say in advance what is to happen and for how long – each person takes part at their own pace, or simply is there
Burn only dry wood, keep the fire small and never leave it unattended
Follow fire bans – then the fire becomes lanterns and candles
Never bathe alone in darkness or cold, and someone always stays on land
Close with thanks and something warm to drink together
hallning_p: What the book describes can be done without believing in anything in particular, and none of it is compulsory. The place says no to radicalism and extremism, whether political or religious, to violence, threats and compulsion, to promises of healing that nobody can keep, and to alcohol and drugs during ceremonies. Ceremonies can awaken strong feelings, but they are not treatment and do not replace care.
forord: This book begins in the dark. Not in January, when the almanac turns its page, but in December, when the day is shortest and most of us would rather sleep through it. It is a deliberate choice. In almost every tradition something new begins in the dark: the seed in the soil, the child in the night, the light lit when it is weakest. Whoever begins the year there need not wait for something to happen. It has already begun.

The Year’s Breath is a calendar for anyone who wants to live the year a little more slowly and a little more attentively. It follows the same fifteen months as the place itself: from the Winter Moon in December 2026, through a whole round of spring, summer and autumn, to the Light Moon in February 2028. Each month has its moon, its festivals, its ceremonies at Vreta and a simple practice that can be done at home, wherever you live.

The book is a companion to The Spirit and keeps step with The Calendar Year. Where The Calendar Year asks what is to be done, this book asks how it can be done with presence. The dates are the same in both.
efterord: Fifteen months is longer than a year and shorter than a life. It is enough to see how much comes back – the light, the moon, the frogs, the cranes – and how little of it is exactly the same the second time. The December the book ends in is not the December it began in, and whoever has followed it is not the same either.

Nothing in the book was difficult. A candle in the window, a walk in silence, a word of thanks before food, a question to carry. That is the point. The spiritual year is not lived in the great moments, but in the small ones repeated until they become a rhythm. The rhythm is not there to make you better. It is there to make you attentive.

Vreta is a small place near Ekoln, and this book is written for it. But the moon is the same over Uppsala as over a flat in Malmö or a cabin in Jämtland, and silence is found wherever someone chooses it. Whoever wants to follow the next round can begin again where they stand. There is always a candle to light and an intention to write.

register.intro: Christianity follows the church year, which begins with Advent and moves through two great cycles of festivals: Christmas, which is reckoned from the sun and has fixed dates, and Easter, which is reckoned from the moon and moves between 22 March and 25 April. Easter Day falls on the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. The Orthodox churches reckon Easter by the old Julian calendar and often celebrate both Christmas and Easter later. In Sweden many church festivals have also become folk festivals, and it is often these that most people recognise.

poster.x: Advent means arrival and is the four Sundays before Christmas, a time of waiting before the birth of Jesus. The church year begins with the first Sunday of Advent. In homes a new candle is lit in the Advent candlestick each Sunday, and in church "Hosanna" is sung. Advent was once a time of fasting. The candles growing in number symbolise the light coming closer, in the middle of the darkest weeks of the year.

St Lucia’s Day remembers Lucy of Syracuse, a Christian martyr of the fourth century, but the Swedish Lucia festival is a blend of saint’s legend and old folk belief about the long Lucia night. It is celebrated with a Lucia procession at dawn or in the evening: a Lucia with a crown of candles, attendants, star boys, songs, saffron buns and coffee. The light in her hair symbolises the promise that the darkness will turn.

Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the story of God becoming human and being born in a stable. In Sweden Christmas Eve is the great day, with the Christmas smorgasbord, the tree and presents, while Christmas Day is the church’s feast day, with julotta early in the morning. Christmas symbolises light born in darkness, gifts and hospitality, and that the holy can be found in the simplest things.

Epiphany remembers the wise men who followed the star to the child, and so that Christ was revealed to the whole world. In Sweden it is a public holiday and ends the feast days of Christmas. The star and the gifts – gold, frankincense and myrrh – symbolise that the holy shows itself to all peoples, and that one seeks the light.

The Orthodox churches that follow the Julian calendar celebrate Christmas thirteen days after the Western one. The celebration is preceded by forty days of fasting and begins with a long service during Christmas night, often with candles and choral singing. Orthodox Christmas emphasises the incarnation, that God becomes human, and that the whole of creation becomes holy.

The twentieth day of Christmas is named after Knud Lavard, a Danish duke and saint. The day marks the end of Christmas in Sweden: the tree is stripped and carried out, ideally with dancing and song. It symbolises that a festival has a beginning and an end, and that everyday life may return.

Candlemas, the Feast of the Purification of the Virgin Mary, remembers when Mary and Joseph presented Jesus in the Temple and old Simeon called the child "a light to lighten the Gentiles". The year’s candles were once blessed in church, hence the name mass of light. The day symbolises the returning light and the half of winter that has passed.

Shrove Tuesday was the last day to eat one’s fill before the Lenten fast, and the semla is what remains of that tradition. Ash Wednesday begins Lent, forty days until Easter, and in many churches a cross of ash is drawn on the forehead. The ash symbolises mortality and repentance: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return."

The Annunciation remembers when the angel Gabriel came to Mary and told her she would bear the son of God, nine months before Christmas. The day normally falls around 25 March, Lady Day, which has given Sweden Waffle Day. It symbolises a yes to the unknown and life beginning in hiding.

Easter is the church’s greatest festival and tells of Jesus’s last days, death and resurrection. Palm Sunday remembers the entry into Jerusalem. Maundy Thursday remembers the Last Supper, when Holy Communion was instituted. Good Friday is the day of the crucifixion, the quietest day of the church year. Easter Saturday is the day of waiting, and Easter Day celebrates the resurrection with joy and light. In Sweden eggs, Easter twigs, Easter witches and the Easter table belong to it. Easter symbolises that life is stronger than death and that something new can rise from what has broken.

The Orthodox churches celebrate Easter by the Julian calendar, this year five weeks after the Western one. The midnight service ends with the light being carried out of the church and passed from candle to candle, and people greet one another with "Christ is risen". Red-dyed eggs are a sign of new life.

Forty days after Easter the church remembers when Jesus was taken up into heaven and left the disciples. In Sweden the day is also the day of gökotta, when people go out at dawn to listen to the birds. It symbolises a farewell that is not a loss, and that the holy is everywhere, not only in one place.

Whitsun is celebrated fifty days after Easter and remembers when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples as tongues of fire, so that they could speak and be understood in many languages. It is counted as the church’s birthday. The fire and the wind symbolise a power that cannot be held, and community across the borders of language.

poster.n: St John the Baptist’s Day and Midsummer
poster.x: The birth of John the Baptist is celebrated on 24 June, half a year before the birth of Jesus. Until 1953, 24 June was also the Swedish Midsummer Day. Midsummer has pre-Christian roots in the celebration of light and growth: the maypole, flower crowns, dancing and seven kinds of flowers under the pillow. It symbolises abundance, fertility and the intensity of the short summer.

St Bridget, born in 1303, was Sweden’s first saint. She founded Vadstena Abbey and wrote down her revelations, and today she is one of the patron saints of Europe. The day is marked with masses and pilgrimages, especially in Vadstena. Bridget stands for the courage to speak, also to power.

St Olaf’s Day, Olsok, remembers the Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson, who fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and became the most revered saint of the Nordic countries. It is celebrated with bonfires and pilgrimages to Trondheim. In Sweden the day belongs to harvest time.

Michaelmas is the day of the Archangel Michael, the angel who by tradition defeats the dragon. In farming society the day was an important boundary: the harvest was to be in and the servants’ year drew to its end. It symbolises the struggle of good against evil and order before winter.

Harvest Thanksgiving is the Church of Sweden’s harvest festival, on the second Sunday in October. The churches are decorated with bread, fruit and vegetables from the area, and the gifts often go on to those in need. It symbolises gratitude for the gifts of the earth and for the work behind them.

All Saints remembers all the saints and all who have died. In Sweden candles are lit on graves and in memorial groves, and the churchyards glow in the November dark. All Saints’ Eve is the day before. The candles symbolise memory and the hope that the dead are not gone.

St Martin’s Eve is linked both to Martin of Tours, who shared his cloak with a beggar, and to Martin Luther, born on 10 November 1483. It is celebrated with goose dinner, above all in Skåne. The goose belongs to the slaughtering season and the last feast before the Advent fast.

poster.n: The Sunday of the Last Judgement
poster.x: The Sunday of the Last Judgement is the last Sunday of the church year and is about the Last Judgement and Christ as king. It is a day for reflection before Advent. It symbolises that everything has an end and that every person is seen.

The Apostle Thomas, the one who doubted, has his day at the longest night of the year. In farming society the Christmas ale was to be brewed: "Thomas with the barrel." The day symbolises that doubt and faith belong together, and that the darkness has reached its lowest point.

The Apostle Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. In folk belief his day was associated with ice: "Matthias breaks the ice; if there is no ice, he makes ice." The day was expected to bring a change in the weather.

register.intro: The Jewish calendar is a lunar calendar kept in step with the sun by adding an extra month seven times in nineteen years. So the festivals move in the Gregorian calendar but always land in the same season. The day begins at sunset, so every festival begins the evening before. The Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, is the most important festival of all and returns every week.

poster.x: Hanukkah remembers how the Temple in Jerusalem was rededicated in the 160s BCE after the Maccabean revolt, and the story of the oil that was enough for only one day but burned for eight. Each evening one more candle is lit in the hanukkiah, the nine-branched candlestick, which is set in the window. Food fried in oil is eaten, such as latkes and doughnuts, and the children play with the spinning top, the dreidel. The lights symbolise that one does not hide one’s faith and that a small light goes a long way.

Tu Bishvat is the New Year of the Trees, the fifteenth day of the month of Shevat. Originally it was a date for reckoning the age of trees when their fruit was to be tithed. Today people eat fruits from the land of Israel – dates, figs, olives, pomegranates – and plant trees. The day has become a festival for nature and the responsibility for it.

Purim celebrates the story in the Book of Esther of how Queen Esther saved the Jewish people in Persia from the minister Haman’s plot. The Book of Esther is read aloud in the synagogue, and every time Haman’s name is mentioned it is drowned out with rattles. People dress up, give gifts of food to friends and money to the poor, and eat a festive meal. Purim symbolises that rescue can come hidden and unexpected.

Pesach, the Jewish Passover, remembers the exodus from slavery in Egypt. At the Seder meal on the first evening the story is told with the help of symbolic dishes: bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery, unleavened bread, matzah, for the haste, and salt water for the tears. During the week no leavened bread is eaten. Passover symbolises freedom and that each generation should see itself as though it had itself come out of Egypt.

Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, is celebrated seven weeks after Passover and remembers when the Torah was given at Mount Sinai. It was also a harvest festival for wheat and the first fruits. Many stay up and study all night, and dairy food is eaten. Shavuot symbolises that the freedom of Passover is given a direction through the teaching.

Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, this year the year 5788. It is also the start of the Ten Days of Repentance. The shofar, a ram’s horn, is blown in the synagogue to rouse people to reflection. Apple dipped in honey is eaten for a sweet year and round bread for the cycle of the year. The new year symbolises a fresh start and that every person may look over their life.

Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. People fast for twenty-five hours, pray for forgiveness and ask others for forgiveness, and many dress in white. The day ends with a last long blast of the shofar. It symbolises cleansing, repentance and the possibility of beginning again.

Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles, remembers the forty years in the desert when the people lived in temporary huts. A sukkah is built with a roof of branches, sparse enough to see the stars, and meals are eaten there. During prayer four plants are waved: palm frond, myrtle, willow and the citron, the etrog. Sukkot symbolises gratitude for the harvest and trust in what is temporary.

register.intro: The Islamic calendar is a purely lunar calendar of twelve months and about 354 days, so the festivals move about eleven days earlier each year and travel through all the seasons in 33 years. Each month begins when the new moon’s first crescent has been sighted, so dates can differ by a day between countries and mosques. The day begins at sunset. 2027 counts as the years 1448 and 1449 after the Hijra, the Prophet Muhammad’s emigration from Mecca to Medina in 622.

poster.d: around 8 February – 9 March 2027 and 28 January – 26 February 2028
poster.x: Ramadan is the ninth month, the month in which by tradition the Qur’an began to be revealed. During Ramadan adult Muslims fast from dawn to sunset: no food, no drink. The day begins with suhoor, a meal before dawn, and the fast is broken with iftar, often with dates and water, and then a meal together. The evenings are filled with prayer and reading. The fast symbolises self-discipline, compassion for those who hunger and closeness to God.

Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, is the night when the first verses of the Qur’an were revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. It falls on one of the last odd nights of Ramadan, usually reckoned as the twenty-seventh. Many spend the night in prayer at the mosque. The Qur’an says that this night is better than a thousand months.

Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast, is celebrated when Ramadan ends. The day begins with communal prayer, and before it zakat al-fitr is given, a gift to the poor so that everyone can celebrate. People dress well, visit family and friends, eat well and the children get presents. Eid symbolises joy, gratitude and community.

Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, is celebrated during the pilgrimage to Mecca and remembers the Prophet Ibrahim’s – Abraham’s – willingness to sacrifice his son and God’s mercy in providing a ram instead. Families who are able slaughter an animal and divide the meat into three parts: for the family, for friends and neighbours and for those in need. The festival symbolises trust, willingness to sacrifice and sharing.

The Islamic New Year, the first day of the month of Muharram, remembers the Hijra, the emigration from Mecca to Medina. The new year is marked quietly, often with prayer and reflection. For Shia Muslims the first ten days of Muharram are a time of mourning that culminates in Ashura.

Mawlid an-Nabi is the Prophet Muhammad’s birthday. Many Muslims celebrate with songs and poems about the Prophet, stories from his life, prayers and meals. Others do not celebrate at all, since they hold that the Prophet himself did not. For those who celebrate, the day symbolises love for the Prophet and a life in his footsteps.

Laylat al-Bara’at, the Night of Forgiveness, falls two weeks before Ramadan. Many Muslims, especially in South Asia, spend the night in prayer, ask for forgiveness and visit graves. The night symbolises cleansing before the month of fasting.

register.intro: Hinduism is not a single doctrine but a multitude of traditions with shared roots in India: the Vedic scriptures, epics such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and gods such as Vishnu, Shiva and the goddess Devi in many forms. The festivals follow a lunar calendar kept in step with the sun, and each day has its tithi, its lunar day. Since a tithi can begin in the middle of a day, dates often differ by a day between regions and almanacs. The dates here follow Drik Panchang for New Delhi. Many festivals are about the same thing in different guises: good triumphing over evil, light over darkness, and the bonds between people, gods and nature.

poster.x: Gita Jayanti celebrates the day when, by tradition, the god Krishna gave the warrior Arjuna the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita, on the battlefield at Kurukshetra. The Gita, seven hundred verses from the Mahabharata, is about acting rightly without binding oneself to the result. The day is marked by reading and reciting the whole text in temples and homes, often with fasting. It symbolises wisdom in the midst of conflict and the duty to act with a calm mind.

Lohri is the last great evening of winter in Punjab, the night before Makar Sankranti, and is celebrated by both Hindus and Sikhs. People gather round a great bonfire, throw sesame seeds, peanuts, popcorn and sweets into the fire, sing and dance bhangra. Families with a newborn child or a newly married couple celebrate especially. The fire symbolises thanks for the harvest and leaving the cold season behind.

Makar Sankranti falls when the sun enters Capricorn, one of the few Hindu festivals that follow the sun rather than the moon. The days grow noticeably longer. In northern India kites are flown, people bathe in sacred rivers and share sweets of sesame and jaggery. In Tamil Nadu Pongal is celebrated at the same time over four days: newly harvested rice is boiled with milk until it boils over, and people cry "Pongalo pongal!". The festival symbolises thanks to the sun and the earth, abundance and a new beginning.

Thaipusam is celebrated by Tamil Hindus at the full moon in the month of Thai, in memory of when the goddess Parvati gave her son Murugan a spear to defeat the demon Soorapadman. Pilgrims fast for weeks and then carry kavadi, a burden that may be a pot of milk or a heavy frame, often with skewers through the skin, to Murugan’s temple. The celebrations are largest in Malaysia, Singapore and southern India. Thaipusam symbolises devotion, penance and the strength to carry what is heavy.

Vasant Panchami is the first day of spring in the Hindu calendar and is dedicated to Saraswati, goddess of knowledge, music, art and language. People dress in yellow like the flowering mustard fields, place books and instruments by her image and pray for wisdom. Children often write their first letters on this day, and kites are flown. The day symbolises learning, creativity and the arrival of spring.

Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, is one of the most important nights in Hinduism. It remembers Shiva’s cosmic dance and his union with the goddess Parvati. Believers fast during the day and keep vigil all night in the temples, where Shiva’s lingam is bathed in milk, water and honey and adorned with bael leaves while the mantra "Om namah shivaya" is sung. The night symbolises overcoming darkness and ignorance within oneself.

Holi is the festival of colours and celebrates the arrival of spring. On the evening before, great fires are lit, Holika Dahan, in memory of the story of the devout Prahlad who came unharmed out of the fire while the demoness Holika burned. The next day people throw coloured powder and coloured water at one another – friends, strangers, old and young – and share sweets. During Holi the differences between people are wiped out for a day. The festival symbolises the triumph of good, the love between Krishna and Radha and the joy of spring.

poster.n: Chaitra Navratri, Ugadi and Ram Navami
poster.x: Chaitra Navratri is spring’s nine nights for the goddess Durga in her nine forms, with fasting and prayer. On the day it begins the new year is celebrated in southern and western India: Ugadi in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra, with a dish that mixes sweet, sour, bitter and hot – all the flavours of life. The ninth day is Ram Navami, the birthday of the god Rama, when the Ramayana is read and temples are decorated. The period symbolises a new beginning and the righteous life Rama stands for.

Hanuman Jayanti celebrates the monkey god Hanuman, Rama’s faithful companion in the Ramayana, who flew across the sea to Lanka to rescue Sita. People visit his temples, anoint his image with orange sindoor and read the Hanuman Chalisa. In southern India he is celebrated at other times of year. Hanuman symbolises devotion, courage, strength and service.

Akshaya Tritiya means "the imperishable third day" and is counted among the most auspicious days of the year. Whatever is begun on this day is said never to end. Many buy gold, give gifts to those in need, marry or start new projects. The day symbolises prosperity and goodness that grows.

Guru Purnima is celebrated at the full moon in the month of Ashadha and is dedicated to the teacher, the guru. It also remembers the sage Vyasa, who by tradition gathered the Vedas and wrote the Mahabharata. Hindus, Buddhists and Jains honour their spiritual teachers and parents with flowers, gifts and thanks. The day symbolises knowledge passed on from person to person.

Raksha Bandhan celebrates the bond between siblings. The sister ties a thread, a rakhi, round her brother’s wrist and prays for him, and the brother promises to protect her and gives a gift. Today rakhi is also tied between cousins, friends and neighbours. The thread symbolises care, protection and a bond that holds.

Janmashtami celebrates Krishna’s birth at midnight, on the eighth day of the waning moon. People fast during the day, sing and read about Krishna’s childhood, and at midnight a small image of the child Krishna is bathed and laid in a cradle. In Maharashtra young people form tall human pyramids to reach a pot of butter, dahi handi, in memory of the mischievous Krishna who stole butter. The festival symbolises divine love and joy.

Ganesh Chaturthi celebrates Ganesha, the elephant-headed god who removes obstacles and is invoked before anything new. Clay figures of Ganesha, from small ones to several metres tall, are brought into homes and marquees and worshipped with song, flowers and sweet modak for up to ten days. Then they are carried in procession and immersed in the sea, rivers or lakes. The festival symbolises new beginnings and that everything that has form also dissolves.

Onam is Kerala’s great harvest festival and is celebrated by everyone, whatever their religion. It remembers the good king Mahabali, under whose rule all were equal and none suffered want, and who comes back every year to visit his people. Flower carpets, pookalam, are laid in front of the houses, snake boats race and people eat sadya, a feast of up to twenty-five dishes served on banana leaves. Onam symbolises abundance, equality and a longing for a just time.

The autumn Navratri is nine nights for the goddess Durga and her battle against the buffalo demon Mahishasura. In Gujarat garba and dandiya are danced in rings all night. In Bengal Durga Puja is the greatest festival of the year, with giant figures of the goddess in pavilions and the high point on the eighth day, Durga Ashtami, on 7 October. The tenth day, Dussehra or Vijayadashami, on 9 October, also remembers Rama’s victory over the demon king Ravana: large figures of Ravana are filled with fireworks and burned. The festival symbolises the triumph of good and the feminine power, shakti.

Diwali, the festival of light, is the greatest festival in Hinduism and is also celebrated by Jains and Sikhs. It lasts five days. Dhanteras on 27 October is the day of prosperity, when something new is bought. The main day, 29 October, at the new moon, celebrates Rama’s return to Ayodhya after fourteen years in exile, and the goddess Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, is welcomed with clay lamps, diyas, in every window, patterns of coloured powder, rangoli, at the door and fireworks. The day after is Govardhan Puja, when Krishna is remembered for lifting the mountain Govardhan to shelter the farmers, and on the last day, Bhai Dooj, sisters pray for their brothers. Diwali symbolises light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance and good over evil.

Chhath is an ancient festival for the sun god Surya and the goddess Chhathi Maiya, celebrated above all in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh. For four days people fast, often without water, and stand in rivers and ponds to offer fruit and sweets to the setting sun and the next morning to the rising sun. The festival symbolises gratitude for the life the sun gives and a rigorous purification.

Kartik Purnima is the full moon of the month of Kartik, one of the holiest of the year. People bathe in the Ganges and other sacred rivers and light lamps. In Varanasi Dev Deepawali, the Diwali of the gods, is celebrated, when the river’s steps, the ghats, glow with hundreds of thousands of lamps. At the same full moon Sikhs celebrate the birth of Guru Nanak. The day symbolises light, purification and the gods descending to earth.

register.intro: Buddhism goes back to Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, who lived in northern India some 2,500 years ago and taught the way out of suffering through insight, compassion and a mindful life. There are three main branches: Theravada in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, Mahayana in China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan, and Vajrayana in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia. Many of the festivals follow the full moon, and the same event may be celebrated on different days in different countries. In Sri Lanka every full moon is a poya day, a holiday for temple visits and meditation. Buddhist festivals are seldom first and foremost about feasting, but about giving, meditating, listening to the teaching and keeping ethical precepts.

poster.x: Bodhi Day, in Japanese Rohatsu, remembers the night when Siddhartha sat under the bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya, faced his inner temptations and awoke at the morning star as the Buddha, the awakened one. In Zen monasteries the day is preceded by a week of intensive meditation. At home some decorate a small tree with lights. The day symbolises awakening and that it is possible for everyone.

Losar is the Tibetan New Year and is celebrated in Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal, Ladakh and the Tibetan diaspora. Before the new year the house is cleaned and the old year’s obstacles are driven out with ceremonies and masked dances in the monasteries. Offerings are set out at the altar, new prayer flags raised, monasteries visited and festive food eaten, such as guthuk, a soup with dough balls. The new year is celebrated for up to fifteen days. It symbolises cleansing, renewal and good resolutions.

Parinirvana Day remembers the Buddha’s death at the age of eighty in Kushinagar and his entry into final nirvana, liberation from birth and death. It is celebrated above all by Mahayana Buddhists, with meditation, readings from the Nirvana Sutra and thoughts of those who have died. Some mark it on 8 February. The day symbolises that all things pass and that death need not be something to fear.

Magha Puja, Sangha Day, is celebrated by Theravada Buddhists at the full moon of the third lunar month. It remembers when 1,250 enlightened monks gathered with the Buddha without having been summoned, and he gave them a summary of the teaching: to avoid evil, do good and purify the mind. In the evening people walk three times clockwise round the temple with candles, flowers and incense, one round each for the Buddha, the teaching and the community. The day symbolises the sangha, the spiritual community.

Vesak is the greatest festival of Buddhism and is celebrated at the full moon in May. For Theravada Buddhists it remembers on the same day the Buddha’s birth, awakening and death. In Sri Lanka it is celebrated on 19 May, in Thailand and India on 20 May. Houses and temples are adorned with lanterns and lights, food is given to monks and to everyone passing by, and many keep eight precepts for the day. In several countries captive birds are set free. Vesak symbolises compassion, generosity and awakening.

Poson Poya is Sri Lanka’s full moon day in June, in memory of when the monk Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka, brought Buddhism to the island in the third century BCE. Pilgrims in white climb the hill of Mihintale, where the meeting is said to have taken place, and food and drink are handed out free along the roads. The day symbolises the teaching passed on and generosity to strangers.

Asalha Puja, Dhamma Day, remembers the Buddha’s first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath, where he taught the Four Noble Truths and set the wheel of the teaching in motion. The day after, 19 July, Vassa begins, the rains retreat: for three months monks and nuns stay in their monasteries for study and meditation, as they have done since the Buddha’s time, when people did not want to trample the crops during the rainy season. Many lay people give something up during the same time, such as alcohol or meat. The retreat symbolises deepening, patience and stillness.

Obon in Japan and Ulambana, the Hungry Ghost Festival, in China and Vietnam rest on the story of the disciple Maudgalyayana, who rescued his mother from suffering by giving gifts to the monks. During Obon the spirits of the ancestors are said to come home: graves are tidied, lanterns lit to show the way, and bon-odori is danced. On the last evening lanterns are set out on rivers and lakes to accompany the spirits back. In China food and incense are offered and paper lanterns float on the water. The festivals symbolise gratitude towards parents and ancestors and compassion for all who suffer.

The rains retreat ends with Pavarana at the full moon in October, when the monks ask one another for forgiveness and to be reminded of their shortcomings. Then follows Kathina, a month when lay people in processions give new robes, cloth and provisions to the monasteries. In Thailand and Laos boats of light are set out on the rivers. The period symbolises humility, reconciliation and the joy of giving.

register.intro: Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab around 1500 and rests on faith in one God, on equality between all people and on work, sharing and prayer. Sikh festivals mainly follow the traditional lunar calendar or the Nanakshahi calendar. Every gurdwara, the Sikh temple, has a langar, a kitchen where everyone eats together whatever their religion, caste or background.

poster.x: Vaisakhi is both a harvest festival in Punjab and the Sikh new year. Above all the day remembers 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, the community of initiated Sikhs. The day is celebrated with worship and processions, nagar kirtan, in which the holy scriptures are carried through the streets with singing, and with langar for all. Vaisakhi symbolises courage, equality and a new beginning.

Guru Nanak Gurpurab celebrates the first guru, the founder of Sikhism. The holy scripture Guru Granth Sahib is read from cover to cover over the forty-eight hours before the day, and it is celebrated with processions, song, lights and langar. The day symbolises Guru Nanak’s message: there is one God, and all people are equal before it.

register.intro: In China, Vietnam, Korea and much of East Asia the traditional festivals follow the lunar calendar. Several traditions meet here: ancestor veneration, Taoism, Buddhism and Confucian ideals of family and duty. The festivals are family festivals, and most are about gathering.

poster.x: Dongzhi is the festival of the winter solstice. From now on the days grow longer, and yang, the force of light and warmth, begins to grow again. The family gathers and eats tangyuan, sweet rice balls in warm soup, whose round shape stands for togetherness and wholeness. In northern China dumplings are eaten instead.

The Lunar New Year, the Spring Festival, is the greatest festival of the year. 2027 opens the Year of the Sheep or Goat and 2028 the Year of the Monkey. The house is cleaned to sweep out bad luck, the doors are decorated with red paper and lucky signs, and the family gathers for a great dinner on New Year’s Eve. The children get money in red envelopes, and fireworks and lion dances frighten away evil. The festival lasts fifteen days and ends with the Lantern Festival. It symbolises renewal, good fortune and the bonds of family.

The Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated at the full moon of the eighth lunar month, when the moon is said to be at its roundest and clearest. The family gathers, looks at the moon, lights lanterns and shares mooncakes, sweet pastries filled with lotus seed or red bean. The legend tells of Chang’e, who lives on the moon. The round moon symbolises that the family is whole – and longing for whoever is far away.

register.intro: The Persian calendar follows the sun, and the year begins when spring does. The festivals are celebrated in Iran and by Persian-speaking and Iranian families all over the world, whatever their religion.

poster.x: Nowruz means new day and is the Persian New Year, celebrated for more than three thousand years by Iranians, Kurds, Afghans and many peoples of Central Asia. It begins at the exact moment spring begins. Homes are spring-cleaned, people jump over fires on the night before the last Wednesday, and the haft-sin table is laid with seven things whose names begin with s – among them sprouted wheat, apple, garlic and vinegar – together with a mirror, candles and painted eggs. Nowruz symbolises spring’s victory over winter and the renewal of life.

register.trad: The Celtic and Nordic wheel of the year
register.intro: The Celts divided the year into four seasonal festivals midway between the solstices and equinoxes, and the Nordic peoples celebrated the turning points of the sun. Much of this lives on in our own festivals – the Walpurgis bonfire, the maypole, Lucia – and in modern times it has been taken up by neopagan and nature-religion movements as the wheel of the year.

poster.x: The winter solstice is the shortest day of the year, when the sun turns. In the pre-Christian north midwinter was marked with blót and feasts, and Christmas has taken over much of it. The solstice symbolises that the light turns at the darkest moment.

Imbolc is the first festival of the Celtic spring, when the ewes lambed and the milk came back. It is sacred to Brigid, goddess and later saint of fire, poetry, healing and wells. Candles are lit, Brigid’s crosses plaited from straw and bread and milk set in the window. Imbolc symbolises the return of the light and the life stirring beneath the earth.

At the spring equinox day and night are the same length, and spring begins astronomically. Many cultures have celebrated it as a festival of new year and fertility. It symbolises balance and the passage from darkness to light.

Walpurgis Night (valborg) is named after the saint Walburga, but the bonfires are older: fires were lit to frighten away predators and evil powers before the cattle were let out. The Celtic Beltane on 1 May is the start of summer, when the cattle were driven between two fires for protection. The fire symbolises cleansing, warmth and the victory of spring.

The summer solstice is the longest day of the year. In the Nordic countries the Midsummer celebration has taken over much of the old solstice festival. It symbolises the height of the light – and that it now turns again.

Lughnasadh is the first harvest festival, named after the god Lugh. The first bread was baked from the year’s grain and shared. In England the day was called Lammas, the loaf mass. It symbolises gratitude for the harvest and for the sacrifice every harvest involves.
At the autumn equinox day and night are once more the same length, and darkness takes over. It is the time of harvest and thanks. It symbolises balance and preparation for rest.

Samhain is often counted as the Celtic new year, when summer ended and winter began. The night was held to be the one when the boundary between the living and the dead was thinnest. Fires were lit, places laid for the dead and people dressed up. Halloween and All Saints bear its traces. Samhain symbolises the end that is also a beginning.

register.intro: The Sámi are an Indigenous people of Sápmi, which stretches across Sweden, Norway, Finland and Russia. The Sámi calendar follows the year of the reindeer, the fishing and the light, and the festivals are carried by the Sámi themselves and their organisations, among them the Sámi Parliament. We describe the days and do not celebrate them in their stead.

poster.x: The winter market in Jokkmokk has been held since 1605 and is a meeting place for trade, handicraft, food and reindeer herding. It is also a Sámi cultural festival with joik, storytelling and reindeer caravans on the ice. The market symbolises that winter in Sápmi is a living season and not only a wait.

On 6 February 1917 the first Sámi national assembly was held in Trondheim, where Sámi from Norway and Sweden met across the borders. Since 1993 the day has been the Sámi National Day. The Sámi flag is raised and the national anthem "Sámi soga lávlla" is sung. The day symbolises a people living in four countries and its right to language, land and culture.

register.intro: In the Andes the relationship of the Inca and Andean peoples to the earth, Pachamama, and to the sun, Inti, lives on in festivals that have often been woven together with Catholic holy days. High in the mountains near Cusco live the Q’ero people, seen by many as bearers of knowledge from Inca times. Their ceremonial leaders, paqos, hold rituals such as the k’intu and the despacho, and these are described month by month in the book.

poster.x: Willkakuti, the return of the sun, is the Aymara people’s new year at the winter solstice in the southern hemisphere. At Tiwanaku in Bolivia people gather before dawn and stretch out their hands towards the first sun. The day symbolises that the light returns and a new year begins.

Quyllur Rit’i, the star snow, is a pilgrimage to the Sinakara valley beneath the mountain Ausangate in southern Peru, around Trinity Sunday. Tens of thousands of pilgrims, among them the Q’ero people, walk there with music and dance. The ukuku dancers, the bears, climb onto the glacier during the night and carry down ice held to be sacred. The pilgrimage unites reverence for the mountains, the apus, with Catholic faith and has been on UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage since 2011. It symbolises renewal and the bond between people, the mountains and the stars.

Inti Raymi, the festival of the sun, was the most important festival of the Inca empire and has been revived in Cusco since 1944. It is celebrated with a great ceremony at the ruins of Sacsayhuamán, with music, dance and offerings to the sun. It symbolises gratitude to the sun and the people’s bond to their origins.

In the Andes August is counted as the month of Pachamama, Mother Earth, when the earth is hungry before the new growing season. People give back: food, chicha, coca leaves and sweets are buried in the earth or burned in a ceremony. The month symbolises reciprocity, ayni – that whoever receives should also give.

In the Inca calendar November was called Aya marq’ay killa, the month when the dead were carried. The ancestors’ mummies were given new clothes, food and drink. Today the tradition lives on in the Andean Todos Santos, when families lay places for their dead, bake t’anta wawa, bread shaped like small children, and gather in the cemeteries. The month symbolises that the dead still belong to the community, the ayllu.

register.intro: In Mexico the older traditions of the Indigenous peoples and Catholic faith meet in festivals celebrated in homes, squares and cemeteries.

poster.x: The Days of the Dead are a meeting between Indigenous Mexican traditions and the Catholic All Saints. The family builds an altar, an ofrenda, with marigolds, candles, photographs and the favourite food and drink of the dead, and visits the graves with music and food. Sugar skulls and skeletons in festive clothes belong to it. The days symbolise that death is part of life and that the dead come visiting when they are remembered.

register.intro: African-American festivals have grown up in the United States during the twentieth century as a way of holding on to African heritage and community.

poster.x: Kwanzaa was established in 1966 by Maulana Karenga as an African-American cultural festival with roots in African harvest festivals. Each evening for seven days a candle is lit in the kinara for one of seven principles, among them unity, self-determination, collective responsibility and faith. The festival ends with a feast, the karamu. It symbolises community, heritage and responsibility.

register.trad: The sacred time of the Maya peoples
register.intro: The Maya peoples of Guatemala and southern Mexico still count the sacred time, the cholq’ij, of 260 days. The count is carried by the daykeepers, ajq’ijab’, in their own communities. Here are some of the days they themselves highlight; we are not daykeepers and hold no ceremonies.

poster.x: Wajxaqib’ B’atz’, 8 Thread, is the day when the K’iche’ Maya’s sacred calendar of 260 days is traditionally celebrated in the highlands of Guatemala. The daykeepers, ajq’ijab’, are initiated and give thanks for time. The ceremonies are held at sacred places with fire, candles, incense and offerings. The thread symbolises time being spun, and life as a weave in which everything hangs together. What we do at Vreta is inspired by the calendar, not part of it.

register.intro: A few days in the calendar belong to no single tradition, but have become days when many gather around the same thing.

poster.x: On 27 January 1945 Auschwitz-Birkenau was liberated. Since 2005 the day has been the UN’s International Day of Commemoration in memory of the victims of the Holocaust, the six million Jews and all the others who were murdered. Candles are lit and names read. The day symbolises the duty to remember, so that it never happens again.

Earth Day has been marked since 1970 and gathers people all over the world around nature and the climate. People plant trees, clean beaches and talk about the future. It symbolises responsibility for the only planet we have.
The UN’s day of peace calls for a day of ceasefire and non-violence. At noon a minute’s silence is held in many places. It symbolises that peace begins with the small.
In 2024 the UN established a day for meditation at the winter solstice. It calls on people to sit still for a while, wherever they are. It symbolises that inner calm is a shared concern.
